speechtext: The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Hon. Sydney Fisher) moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 184) further to amend the Patent Act. He said : In introducing this Bill, I think that perhaps a short explanation is due to the House. The immediate necessity for the passage of an Act of this character is due to the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada last December in the case of Power vs. Griffin, the effect of which decision has been to alter materially the practice of the department, and in some cases to throw a doubt upon the validity of certain acts of the department in the past. The Bill provides for various other amendments to the Patent Act which have been asked for by the applicants for patents and by those who are practising as patent solicitors in Canada. The Bill provides first of all, to remove doubts raised by the decision of the Supreme Court as to the powers of the deputy commissioner of patents or the acting deputy commissioner of patents. While the decision of the court itself did not involve any question as to the powers of these two officials, still there was an expression of opinion by some of the judges that the deputy commissioner and the acting deputy commissioner had been performing certain acts which they considered to be only within the purview of the commissioner himself.
What are these acts ?

The granting of extension of time for manufacture in the country, and extension of time for importation under the Patent Act. The Bill also makes an important amendment as to the duration of the existing Canadian patents. At present, under our patent law, all Canadian patents cease, determine and are void whenever a similar patent in a foreign country becomes void for any reason whatever. That is a relic of by-gone patent legislation. It has already been removed from the law of Great Britain and the United States and other foreign countries, and those who are connected with the administration of the patent law in Canada believe that Canadian patents ought not to become void simply because of the voiding of the same patents in a foreign country. This amendment will make the existence of the Canadian patents entirely independent of the life of the same patents in foreign countries. We have found in the administration of the patent law that certain difficulties have arisen in the way of the voiding of patents because of non-manufacture
114}

in this country- There is a pretty large class of patents, the manufacture of which is practically impossible until a demand arises for them. A patent for a graving dock is an example. There might be no necessity for the building of a graving dock in Canada for many years after the period of the patent had expired because of nonusage. There are other patents for processes, the manufacture of which is not necessary unless the article, the use of which the process is required for, is manufactured in the country. It seems to be an injustice to the patentee that because of the non-use of the patent in this country the patent should become null and void. In Great Britain they have adopted a system of licensing, and this Bill proposes to apply the British license system to this class of patent when the owner of the patent applies for it, and when, in the judgment of the commissioner of patents, it is a proper patent to allow that licensing system to prevail in regard to, instead of the patents becoming null and void because of the non-use or nonmanufacture of the article in this country. Then, as the decision of the Supreme Court of Canada has shown that certain acts of the deputy commissioner of patents and the acting deputy commissioner of patents were beyond their powers, this Act will render valid acts which have been so performed by these officers. We further propose to revive certain patents which were void, either through failure to manufacture in the country, or by reason of the permission not to manufacture having been given by the officers of the department in a way which this decision of the Supreme Court says was illegal and ineffective.
Hon. Mr. HAGGAllT. How far do you make your ex post facto legislation valid, and to what cases does It apply 1

I will explain that further in detail. I was going over the Bill first. Then we propose another radical amendment in the administration of the office, which has really not occasioned any great trouble, but might do so at any time. The present patent law provides that all papers in connection with patents should be open to public inspection. That provision applies to applications for patents before the patent has been granted. There is no doubt that under that interpretation of the law there is a danger that a person who has filed an application for a patent, a paper which ought to be confidential, might have his patent stolen from him by reason of that fact. We remove the applications for patents from the operation of that section of the law, and make them confidential just as caviats are. until the application has been dealt with and passed upon by the department There is also a provision, not to change, but to make clear the tariff in regard to the fees on the re-issue of a patent. These have been a subject of dispute, and patent solicitors who Hon. Mr. FISHER.
appear before the office have generally considered that the ruling of the office was not indicated clearly by the wording of the Act, and I wish to make the wording of the Act so as to indicate more clearly the ruling of the office, which has been sustained and upheld. There is also a clause to extend the time within which the Commissioner of Patents, under certain circumstances, may be able to give a permit for an extension of time to import. We have clauses conserving the rights of people who may have acquired rights through the decision of the Supreme Court, the results of which by this Act are to be modified to a certain extent. We propose to retroactively maintain and make valid certain patents which at the present time are null and void. We conserve the rights which were acquired during the period in which those patents were not valid. The hon. member (Hon. Mr. Haggart) has asked me particularly in what way we make the Act retroactive. I think the first clause, which deals with that is clause 9 :
The validity of any extension heretofore granted or assumed to be granted under subsection 2 of section 37 of the said Act, of the period of two years limited by that section, or by that section as heretofore amended, for the commencement of the construction or manufacture of a patented invention, or of the period of twelve months thereby limited for the importation of the patented invention, shall not be open to impeachment, because-
(a.) Such extension was so granted or assumed to be granted by the Deputy Commissioner of Patents, or, as acting Deputy Commissioner of Patents, by a person performing the duties of Deputy Minister of Agriculture under the provisions of the Civil Service Act in that behalf, instead of by the Commissioner of Patents; or because
(b.) In the case of the invention to which such extension relates, there had been granted or assumed to be granted a previous ^extension or previous extensions of the period of two years or the period of twelve months, as the case may be, so limited.
The Supreme Court of Canada has decided that while one extension of time may be permitted, no more can be granted by the Commissioner of Patents. It had been the practice of the department to grant more than one extension. This Act will make valid the extensions which have been granted. but, of course, the practice of the department will now change, and only one extension will be granted in each case.
' How about rights acquired by the voiding of a patent ?
There is a general provision carefully preserving all acquired rights under the law.
Suppose a patent lapsed this year, could that be revived in two years from now ?
No. The Bill only makes valid the patents which have lapsed up to the period when
Are you changing the old Act ?

Yes. the reading of the old Act is entirely different because the decision of the Supreme Court completely controverts and overrides Dr. Taclie's decision of 1877. And liecnuse the Supreme Court holds that the decision upon which the patent law has been administered ever since was erroneous and incorrect. This section provides that the patents still in existence, the holders of which have complied with Dr. Taclie's decision, shall be rendered valid, provided that within a fixed time they do what the new reading of the law requires. It is only right that those patents which have become void through the patentee following Dr. Tache's decision should be given an opportunity of lining made valid again.
How will you give the patentees notice ?
That would be a matter of administration. But I should think that the passage of the law and its appearance in the statutes would give most people sufficient notice.
It gives technical notice, but I mean actual notice.

We could undertake, though it would be
great labour, to send notices to the patentees, whose addresses we have, but there are a great many with whom we have had no communications and whose addresses we do not know.
How many patents are voided by this decision of the Supreme Court ?
There are so many patents voided on one ground or another that I could not tell off hand.
In the case of a patent, the manufacture of which has not begun at the expiration of the two years, does this extend the time ?

It gives them six months to comply with the new reading of the law. This Bill also makes valid patents which have expired through the expiry of foreign patents. That is another way in which it is retroactive, of course providing the safeguard of acquired rights. There is a general clause in the Bill giving protection to acquired rights under every provision of this measure, and the Department of Justice and my own deputy minister, who is a lawyer, considers that the clause, as it is drawn, will preserve any acquired rights under any retroactive provisions of this Bill. I may say that this decision of the Supreme Court was quite unexpected, that the jurisprudence of the Patent Law had been maintained on the lines I have beeil discussing some 26 years, and it was only last December that a change was made. I may say that the Department of Justice and my own deputy minister concur fully in the ruling of the Supreme Court, but at the same time I think that the continuous existence of a condition of affairs based on a wrong reading of the law in the department, proves that it was high time that an experienced lawyer was made deputy minister, and I am very glad that I was able to secure the services of an experienced and sound lawyer for the position. I am satisfied that such an appointment will conduce to the more satisfactory administration of these branches - in which legal knowledge is required.
Will it be necessary to come forward with a private Bill in order to renew lapsed patents ?

Most of the private Bills which come lie-fore the House to make valid lapsed patents owe their existence to the neglect of the patentees themselves. This Bill does not deal with any ease in which the patentee has been simply neglectful, but we are trying to remedy a condition of affairs, the existence of which is due to the action of the department and not to the negligence of the patentees. The House will still have the power to pass a private Bill in order to make valid any patent, but this Bill only

affects certain classes of patents which have become void owing to the action of the department.
I understood the hon. gentleman to say that he had appointed a lawyer as Deputy Minister of Agriculture. Does not the work of the patent officer devolve almost entirely on the chief clerk ?

No, the work of the patent branch is directly under the deputy commissioner of patents, who is also the Deputy Minister of Agriculture. True the chief clerk has charge there just as chief clerks have in other branches, but at the same time it is first of all the minister acting through his deputy, the commissioner of patents, who has direct responsibility and control over the work. One of the chief parts of the work of the Deputy Minister of Agriculture,- as now constituted and for a long time back, is to deal with these non-agricultural portions of the work of the department. As my hon. friend knows very well, experts and specialists have charge of the various agricultural branches of the Department of Agriculture, but there has not been anybody of that character in the non-agricultural parts of the department. Therefore it is necessary that somebody should be able to deal with these things as a deputy minister.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to mention to the Prime Minister a fact that I have already brought to his attention. So far as this House is concerned, no documents whatever relating to the colonial conference have ever been brought down. It is true that a few members of parliament have been able to procure a copy of the documents which were laid on the Table of the Imperial House, but so far as this House is concerned, it is in absolute ignorance of any of the results of that colonial conference, unless the documents have been brought down some time during my absence. I mentioned this to the right lion, gentleman some time ago, and I understood from him at that time that there was no objection to bringing down the documents so that every one of them1 might be available and in the hands of every member of this House. It seems to me that is a very reasonable proposition. I would like, therefore, to ask the right hon. gentleman whether, there is any objection to that. Also I would be glad if he would bring down any such documents that have not been laid on the Table of the imperial parliament and that may particularly concern the interest of this country as represented at the colonial conference. I would also ask that when the documents are brought down they should be printed with as much expedition as

possible, so that they may be in the hands of lion, members on both sides of the House before the conclusion of the session.

I may say to my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) that there are no other documents to be brought down or In existence than those contained in the Imperial Blue-book. With regard to the advisability of having the blue-book printed for the information of the members of the House, that is a reasonable request, and steps shall be taken immediately with that object in view.

Now, let me depart for one moment from a further examination of the conditions and operation of the railway for the past year, to give you a statement, so far as, and down to as late a period as, it is possible to make it out, of the operations for the current year. The statement which I am about to furnish brings us down to the end of the month of March. We have not yet received a statement of the results down to the end of April. I give them to the House as far as they are available. Our earnings for the nine months just past of the current year run up to $4,745,000. The receipts for the corresponding period of last year were $4,184,000, an increase of $561,000 in the gross earnings for the nine months of the current year. For the same period this year the working expenses were $4,775,000, as compared with $4,187,500 for the corresponding period of last year, an increase of $570,000. The earnings for the nine months were $4,745,000, the working expenses for the nine months were $4,775,500. The excess of working expenses over earnings was $30,500. On the 31st March last year, we had a deficit of $60,000, while on the 31st March, 1901 we had a deficit of $130,000, and yet at the end of the fiscal year 1902, we had the surplus which I have stated of $96,800. Now, I may, perhaps, take a moment to furnish the House with a little explanation as to why this ordinarily occurs.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Before passing from that would the hon. gentleman say what was the amount expended upon capital account up to March 31st ?

I must beg my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) not to interrupt me on the question of capital at this stage. The question of capital does not alter this statement nor its bearing to the extent of a hair's breadth.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It was just for my own information.
I am not taking into account one copper of capital outlay in any particular.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It was for my own information, and not for the purpose of affecting the hon. gentleman's argument at all. If the hon. gentleman has it. I would like to have it, but if he has not, I do not wish it.

I would not hesitate to give it to the hon. gentleman now, but it would be very inconvenient to break into the statement and speak about the amount expended Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
upon capital account. I will give the hon. gentleman the information in due course.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I wish to apologise to the hon. gentleman. He was giving the amount expended and the receipts, and I thought perhaps, in the same table from which he got the information, the officers of the department would have given the total amount of the expenditure.

I am endeavouring to give a statement of the amount which goes into consolidated revenue account, or in other words, the gross earnings of the road on one side and the expenditure incurred in the operating of the railway on the other, and so far as the question of capital expenditure is concerned, it does not in the remotest degree affect the matter one way or the other. If we had spent less money in maintaining the railway, and if a comparison had been made between previous years and this past year, and it appeared from that comparison that I had expended less money in the maintenance of the road, and that I had taken money from capital account and spent it for the purpose of keeping up the road, then I could understand the relevancy of my hon. friend's desire to get this information. It does not bear upon it in any particular at all. I have shown that we spent upon the actual operation of the railway out of earnings, not out of capital, $500,000 more than was expended in 1896, which is a fair average year under the hon. gentleman's administration. I claim the benefit of the comparison. I have shown that we were in a much better position in operating the railway in 1902 than my hon. friend was in 1896.
When my hon. friend interrupted me. I was about to offer an explanation. There is a portion of the year in which the road is more expensively operated than in other portions of the year, and when the business is not as flourishing as during other months. It happens that during the winter months, December, January. February and running into March, it costs more to maintain and operate the line, and that the business is not usually so large: so that every year you make a poorer showing to the end of March than you are able to make when the year closes, because, after that, your expenses for maintenance are less and your receipts are larger. We were able in 1902 to convert what had been a deficit of $60,000. on the 31st March, into a surplus of $96,800 on the 30th June. My estimate is that at the end of the present fiscal year we will be able to show, everything going well, and from present indications I think I can speak with some confidence, a surplus of at least $125,000. It is fair to call the attention of the House to the important and significant fact to which I have just pointed, that out of the earnings which came from the traffic of the

railway in the year 1902, we spent in the same proportion which had been spent under the previous administration, aud we had out of these earnings $500,000 more which we were able to spend in the same direction for the betterment and improvement of the road. If we had spent no more, and 1 want to impress that fact, because it is a significant fact, upon the attention of the House-if we had spent no more in the maintenance and in improvements upon the road and its equipment than had been spent by our predecessors, I would have been able to come down to parliament and say that instead of having a surplus of .$90,800 I had a surplus of $596,000.
My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) laughs at that, but there is no ground upon which he can ridicule that statement. Where did the money come from ? It did not come from the skies. It did not come from capital; it did not come from the issue of bonds; it was not given to us-it was earned; earned by the carriage of the traffic upon the road. We earned $500,000 more or we would not have been able to expend $500,000 more. That is a significant fact, therefore, because the road is better by $500,000. Mark you, when I speak of the $500,000, I am not speaking of money that has been spent in earning the receipts which come from the carriage of traffic; I am speaking of money that has been spent upon the equipment and the betterment of the road. And if we bad the money to spend it must come out of the earnings, and if it came out of earnings, as it undoubtedly did come, then we must have been able to manage the road and carry the traffic upon the road under more favourable conditions than my hon. friend (Hon. John Haggart) was able to do. If the hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. 'Haggart) had spent $500,000 upon betterments and improvements in 1896, he would have had a deficit of $555,000 instead of a deficit of $55,000. There is no getting away from that; the fact is too clear to need elaborate argument to support it.
If there were no other fact to which I could call the attention of this House and of the country in pointing to our efficient administration of the Intercolonial Railway, I would be able to claim from this fact alone that the Intercolonial Railway had certainly come under an improved management, and is showing greatly improved results. But. before I conclude, Sir. I hope to be able to point to a number of other convincing facts which will serve to impress upon the mind of parliament and upon the mind of the people of the country, the fact that the condition of the Intercolonial Railway has been, under our management, improved year after year until it presents a more favourable spectacle to-day than ever before in its history. Let me give some of the details which go to make up this item of working expenses and which are entirely included within that class of working expenses which mean the improvement
of the roadbed and the improved equipment of the railway. I have calculated these upon the basis of the same number of miles operated as in 1896, because I want to be absolutely fair to my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart). I want to treat him as though he had been handling a railway of exactly the same mileage as I am handling. Any other comparison would not be fair, and I do not want any comparison which is not fair, because being unfair it would militate against the value and force of the statement which I shall make. I take the actual expenditures which the hon. gentleman made in 1896 for the purpose of improving and maintaining the railway, and I add to that expenditure 15 per cent, which is [DOT] the difference between the mileage then and now. Taking the different items of these accounts which I will read to the House, and comparing them with my own, I will be able to show where the improvement comes in.

speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Hear, hear.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS ANI) CANALS. I have been surprised to hear one hon. gentleman opposite who is a keen critic of the Intercolonial Railway, and of the railway administration of the government, and who has had, as I am informed, a good deal of experience with regard to railway administration in some form or other; I was surprised to hear him state that in his opinion it cost $1.10 -to earn every dollar that is earned on the Intercolonial Railway. Perhaps that statement was not made seriously and perhaps the hon. gentleman did not intend it to be taken seriously, but he made the statement with all seriousness in appearance, and I think he was not unwilling that the impression should be entertained in the country this government railway was in the lamentable condition that the more business it did the worse it was off, and that for every dollar we earned on the road we were actually laying out $1.10. Perhaps the hon. gentleman can throw some light upon that matter now. But, if the statement be true, let us see what is the result of it. In 1896 with $3,000,000 worth of business, there was a deficit of $55,000, and his conclusion would be that with the same amount of money expended in proportion upon the road, and upon equipment, and in various other ways in connection with the operating of the railway, we might properly show, without being subject to criticism, a deficit of $110,000 on $6,000,000 worth of business, figuring on the results obtained on the Intercolonial Railway during the last year of the Conservative administration. If with $3,000,000 of business there is a deficit of $55,000, with $6,000,000 of business there should be a deficit of $110,000. But what was the actual result ? It was not, as my hon. friend, with his $1.10 theory, would have us believe. If his theory was correct, and if on $3,000,000 of business, $55,000 was a proper deficit, then on $3,000,000 more business, you would have to add $300,000 more deficit-a total deficit of $355,000. My h'on. friend would have us believe that that might have been the result of the administration of this railway by the government. The actual result, however, for the year ending the 30th of June last, was $96,000 of a surplus, after $520,000 odd had been expended for betterments and improvements over and beyond what was laid out by my predecessor, and $55,000 to he added as representing the deficit which

the hon. gentleman had in 1896. You can , thus see, without going into any further figures or making any closer inspection of the situation, what the difference was between the two administrations. $670,000 is the difference between the operation of the railway under existing conditions, and its operation under the conditions which my hon. friend experienced.
Now, it is only fair to say that it may be held while it costs you a certain amount of money to operate the railway with gross earnings of $3,000,000, it ought not to cost you relatively as much when you are earning $G,000,000, because the fixed charges would be only. very slightly increased in earning the additional $3,000,000. I want to put the case quite fairly, as my hon. friend would put it. While some allowance would have to be made for that consideration, in the case of an ordinary corporation railway, it is not time to any considerable extent with respect to the Intercolonial, and I will tell you why. A corporation railway has its bonds and its stock dividends to pay; its bonded obligation is a fixed charge, which does not increase with the increase of business. Therefore, it would not be fair to expect such a railway to show equally favourable results on a small business as on a large. But In the case of the Intercolonial, we have no bonded obligations.
No interest to pay.

There is no interest to pay ; there are no fixed charges or, if there are any, they are very trifling. The general head pffce expenses are the only fixiedl charges which would remain whether the business increased or diminished. But these would amount to a very trifling sum and would not be sufficient to vary or alter the calculation in any material degree. But I maintain that I am entitled, in the judgment of any person who is at all disposed to consider this question with a fair mind, to have him ask, To what is it due that these larger results have been achieved ? Why is it that these large expenditures out of earnings have been possible ? To what is it due ? That is the question. I have pointed out that it is not due to any sum of money which the government have borrowed on the public credit and handed over to the officers of the Intercolonial to be expended.
I have shown you that there was but one source from which the money came-the surplus earnings over the cost of carrying and handling the goods ; and I am entitled,
I think, to claim some credit for that, and I will show you where and how and why these improved results have been achieved.
One of the reasons is, I frankly confess it, because we have made a connection with Montreal. That the connection has been made is, I think, due to the more favourable view which the government have taken of the Intercolonial Railway than was taken

by our predecessors. For the readiness with which the government took up that project and made the effort to bring about better results on the railway, I think we are entitled to credit. That extension has already begun to bear fruit, though not to the full extent which we have a right to expect in the future. But the railway has made progress, and has achieved large results, and one of the means by which this has been brought about has been the extension to Montreal. Another has been the improvement or modernization of the road. That has done perhaps more than any other one thing to produce a larger percentage in the earnings over the cost of carrying and handling the freight. Let me just pause for a moment to show in one particular how much the modernization of the road has done.
The putting of larger locomotives capable of hauling heavier loads upon the railway has cut down enormously the cost of carrying and hauling the freight. I cannot too strongly enforce on the mind of parliament or on the people of the country this conviction, which is founded on absolute verity, that when the Intercolonial was running with little engines of from 45 to 50 tons, capable of hauling only 180 or 200 tons of freight, they required the same staff and practically the same cost of fuel and management that is required to carry from 800 to 1,000 tons. The margin of wages is a large and most important item in the whole account. When I tell you that in the outlay for working expenses, which has been stated to amount to $5,700,000 for last year, labour amounts to $3,500,000, you will see how large an element the question of wages is in this matter ; and when you are able to handle and carry freight in much larger quantities with the same expenditure of labour, you are beginning to achieve results that can be achieved in no other way. When I think over the matter, I become alarmed at the possibilities which lay before the Intercolonial if the condition of things which existed down to 1896 had been suffered to continue.
If the same volume of business we are now carrying had then been forced upon us, and if we had been compelled to handle it with the same kind of equipment and under the same conditions as then existed, our deficit would have been more likely a million per year instead of $55,000. With the extra equipment we have provided, we are able, on the same mileage, to do to-day a larger percentage of business and make a larger profit. My hon. friend was short of cars. In saying this I have no desire to cast any reflection upon his management, for nothing else could have been expected. But he certainly had not sufficient to do the business, because I find that he was paying from $60,000 to $80,000 per year, if my memory does not fail me, on car mileage to other companies. We have
changed that. To-day we pay a little car mileage but very much less. I think we pay $50,000 per year less than the hon. gentleman did. We pay this much less because we have the cars. We had to get them and we bought them very largely on capital account, but it paid us to do so. Calculate three per cent on all the cars we have bought, and you will find that we save in car mileage sufficient to pay the interest on what these cars cost, which I think is very good and defensible business. My hon. friend had a balance of car mileage against him, and I had for some time also a balance against me, of from $60,000 to $72,000 per year. That represents what we had to pay other railway companies for the use of tlieir cars when we had not sufficient of our own. During my hon. friend's administration and during a portion of my own, that amounted to from $60,000 to $72,000 per year. Well, Mr. Speaker, last year we had $16,SOO to our credit on this account, so that we had made enough to wipe out the deficit in respect to car mileage and leave us $16.SOO besides, making a total saving of $82,000.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Do I understand my hon. friend to say that there was a balance of $60,000 to $72,000 per year against us ?

I do not say against my hon. friend's administration alone because I had the same experience during some years, but as fast as we were able to get the new cars and put them on the line, the balance was lessened. We had to get the cars or we could not do the business, but the business we did warranted the expenditure, because last year we had a surplus to our credit, on the car mileage account of $16,800. Adding $16,800 to the average balance against us in the years I have referred to. and you get $82,000 as the actual saving effected between the former period and the present, and $82,000 comes very near paying the interest on $3,000,000 on freight cars alone.
Incidental to our putting ourselves in a position to do the business that was offering and to do it without absolute loss, we not only had to get heavier engines, but all the other essentials to placing heavier engines-on the road had to be attended to. We could not begin to economize in our management until we got heavier rails, stronger bridges, longer sidings, larger engine houses, larger turning tables, improved equipment in all respects, and in addition put on a dining service with a better class of cars, which has borne results of a most fruitful character. But all this cost money. The results are the strongest possible proof of the wisdom of the policy we have adopted. They show that had we not pursued that course, we would have covered ourselves with absolute discredit as respects the ownership and the operation of the Intercolonial Railway.

I have by no means exhausted the extent of the showing which I am entitled to claim. I had furnished me by the general manager a carefully prepared statement of the conditions which existed in 1896 ns compared with 1902, in regard to the cost of material, supplies, wages and other items, whicli go to make up working expenses. In 1896 the same number of employees, the same quantity of materia), and all the other matters of expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway cost, compared with 1902, much less, and if I can prove this, I am entitled to all the benefits resulting from such comparison. I show you a surplus for the year ending 1002 of about $96,000, and I am able to do this notwithstanding the fact that we paid in wages last year on the Intercolonial Railway $240,000 more money than was paid in 1896 in respect of precisely the same number and class of employees. I am not seeking to make an unfair comparison, but am comparing the wages of exactly the same number and the same class of employees as the hon. gentleman had in 1896; and I tell this House that, in respect of that same number and that same class we took out of earnings in 1902, $240,000 more than he did in 1896 and distributed it among the employees. If we had not shown better results than my hon. friend was able to show-and this is the point I wish to make-we would have had a deficit of about $140,000 instead of any surplus whatever. The wages we pay are not excessive; no man will say that we pay more than we ought to pay or more than other railways are paying. But, if we paid $240,000 more in 1902 than the hon. gentleman paid for the same number and class of employees in 1896, I am entitled to claim that our showing for last year is $240,000 better than his would have been under the same conditions. Now, I come to the item of coal. On the same quantity of coal that was consumed on the road under my hon. friend's administration, we had to pay $150,000 more than he had to pay. That is so much additional charge on the road. If things were not improved in the administration some way or other, we should have been that much behind. And I would ask you to consider this point in this connection-and perhaps I should have mentioned it before-there has been no increase in the rates. We are earning no more for carrying a ton of freight than we did before; the charge is the same. The business may increase, the cost of material may be enhanced, wages may rise, but the tariff for carriage of traffic on the Intercolonial Railway remains stationery, and we must figure it on that basis-we cannot raise it because our expenses are higher. Hon. gentlemen opposite and their supporters and their press would be the first to raise an outcry against us did we add anything to the tariff of the Intercolonial, and the political consequences, the disadvantages to
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: us and the advantages to them, would be so important that no government would think of undertaking it.
Do I understand the hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) to say that l'ates are no higher now than they were in 1896 ?

Yes, I do. I state to my hon. friend (Mr. Bell) that the rates are no higher now than they were in 1896. There may be an instance or two, some trifling particular, in which, in view of special circumstances, they are changed; but I am making a general statement with respect to this, and I say without fear of successful contradiction-I think I ought to know if it were otherwise-that the rates are the same practically now as they were in 1896, in fact the same as they have been ever since the Intercolonial was established and put into operation. They may be a little lower in some particulars than they were at first, but they certainly are no higher. I have stated that we spent $151,000 more for coal than did our predecessors. Then, for stores and supplies of the same quantities and kinds that were procured in 1896, the prices in 1902 applied to that quantity would have caused an increased expenditure of $131,000. So, we have these three items- $241,000 for wages, $151,000 for coal and $131,000 for stores. Add these to the $521,000 spent in bettering the road and you have over a million dollars actually paid out in the year 1902 over and above the proportionate expenditure of 1896. And they had a deficit of $55,000 while we, notwithstanding all, have a surplus of $96,000.
Now, it may not, perhaps, be of great interest to the House, but I would like to make the statement that, if my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) as head of the department that had to employ on the Intercolonial in 1896 as many men as the increased traffic has made it necessary for us to employ in 1902, the amount he would have had us pay over his actual expenditure would have been not merely $240,000 but far more. Mr. Pot-tinger had a very careful examination made and he tells me that applying the rate of wages of 1896 to the present entire staff of the Intercolonial for the current year, the total amount of our increased payments of wages is $1,075,000-a very significant fact indeed.
Now, there is, no doubt, a very widespread impression with regard to the Intercolonial, that, because it is owned and operated by the government, it must necessarily be a failure so far as financial results are concerned-that no government can hope to make a good financial showing with regard to the operation of any railway it owns. I hold that no such sweeping condemnation is justified by anything that has ever occurred with regard to the management or operation of the Intercolonial Railway. It is unjust to the Intercolonial, and I do not

think the people of the country wish to form any unjust opinion, or to condemn the government railway unjustly, but would be glad to welcome facts which would disprove and disabuse their minds of any such erroneous view. It is not fair to condemn the management of the Intercolonial because large financial results have not been achieved in times past-and I include my hon. friend (.Hon. Mr. Haggart) and his party in this general statement-because it is a government railway and is managed under government supervision. I do not think that the general idea prevails now to any extent which did prevail so largely, that political influences and political pressure and all these pulls that were alleged to exist upon the government railway, exist at present. In the first place I deny that they exist, but suppose they do exist, they are not reflected in any material degree in the results of the operation of the road.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

My hon. friend says hear, hear. He knows that so far as it is humanly possible, the Intercolonial is not a political machine, it never has been a political machine to my knowledge within the past six or seven years. The officers of the Intercolonial are not allowed to issue passes and distribute them at election times to one political party, or to any political party. People who want to use the Intercolonial, whether Liberals or Conservatives, during election times are treated precisely upon the same basis, and they have got to pay for their excursion tickets if they want to travel over the road. There is no discrimination, and as regards political influence the operations' of the railway suffer very little harm indeed from that cause. I will tell the House why In nearly all the branches of the management of that railway the staff is organized upon a basis that recognizes seniority and merit for promotion. You have got to start at the bottom. You cannot put one man over the heads of other men who are his seniors in service, or who have more merit. That system exists today in almost the entire service. Therefore, the field for political influence is very limited, except in respect to appointments for the first places, and there it is legitimate and proper. But when recommendations are made to the officials of the road by our friends to fill vacancies that may occur, before any of these people can be appointed they have to submit to .a test to show they are qualified to discharge the duties, and if they are not. I do not think they are retained in the service. So you cannot say that political influences are in operation.
But if political influences are so harmful as they are alleged to be in the government management of railways, how is it that government railways are so frequent in other countries ? Not only are the sweeping inferences which people draw with regard
to the inefficiency of government management not warranted by the facts, but I will prove to a demonstration that even if there were political influences, they are not reflected in the financial results. If government railway management of railways is successful in other countries, why should it not be so in Canada? What is there in the condition of Canada that makes it an exception to all rules 1 Why is it that government railways can be operated in the four corners of the world, in Europe, Asia and Africa, in Italy, in Germany, in the Australian colonies, where governments own roads and operate them successfuly, and they cannot be operated successfully in Canada ? Take Australia ; the government railways show a profit of three and a half or four per cent upon the cost, and their railways as a rule cost twice as much to build as the Intercolonial has cost this country. Why is it that other countries can do this successfully ? Will anybody pretend to argue that there is not as much political pressure brought to bear in the management of government railways in Australia, or South Africa, as there is in Canada ? Why, Sir, there can be no justification for any such statement. There is no reason in the world why Canada should be singled out, why any one should say that while in all other parts of the world government railways are ,operated successfully, they are not operated successfully in Canada. The assertion that here political influence is detrimental to the efficiency and utility of government roads is not founded on fact ; it is a delusion, it is a prejudice. I would like to see that prejudice rooted out, because so long as it exists it is injuring the country, it is injuring our own institutions, and it is calculated to do a great deal of harm to Canada in the future.
Now, somebody may say : Why, in Australia the people were so dissatisfied with the government management that they changed the system and put their railways in the hands of a commission. Well, I believe some of them did so, but not all. There was dissatisfaction, but they did not pro-I)ose to give up control of their railways altogether ; they proposed that the people should continue to hold them. But what occurred in Australia and New Zealand was this-I know it occurred in New Zealand. They found that under government administration they were building more railways than were really needed, they were building them in portions of the country where they were not self-sustaining, where there was not sufficient business to justify their construction. The public decided to try the experiment of putting the management in the hands of a railway commission. They tried the experiment and continued it for a few years, put not finding any better financial results, the consequence was that in 1893 the people came to the conclusion to go back to government management, and that is where they are to-day. All the time, how-

364S
ever, whether the roads were under government management or under a commission, the result was that they paid a substantial return, sometimes larger and sometimes smaller, a substantial percentage of interest upon the outlay. I said that the railways in Australia cost twice as much to build as they do in Canada. In some cases they have cost $75,000 to $80,000 per mile, as compared with about half that cost on our own railways.
Now, when I am told that the Intercolonial does not pay, that as a general thing there is a deficit, that the income hardly ever meets the working expenses, I ask :	Do
you think that is due to the fact that it is a government institution ? If you do, figure out what other roads are paying on the cost. We will say they are paying three or four per cent. Some roads, the Canadian Pacific Railway for instance. I suppose is paying five per cent. Why does not the Intercolonial pay an equal return upon the cost, somebody may ask. Well, three per cent upon the cost of the Intercolonial would amount to something over $2,000,000. Sir, will any sane man suppose, after reflecting a moment, that the difference between operating that road by the government and operating it by a company, maintaining the same rates, would amount to the sum of $2,000,000 in net results ? Is there anybody so intensely prejudiced against the management of the Intercolonial by the government as to suppose that if this road were in the hands of a private corporation, and if that private corporation could not charge any heavier tolls than the Intercolonial does, that instead of having a surplus of $96,000, it would have a surplus of over $2,000,000 ?. In other words, $2,000,000 and upwards a year is wasted by reason of government ownership and because of political pressure. That is what it means. If it does not mean that, what does it mean ?
I am going to ask the House to follow me through an examination of the question because I think it is of such importance as to warrant an examination, and we will see how much more economically other roads are being operated than the government road and what greater results they show than the government not only at present, but in times past as well. I am not going to distinguish against hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House and in my own favour in this statement I am about to make. We paid $5,574,000 last year for working expenses. The political enormity, the devastation which results from government ownership must find itself somewhere within that $5,574,000 of working expenses because the working expenses would have to be reduced by $2,000,000 before you could get any $2,000,000 results. These $2,000,000 must represent the extravagance, 'syaste and mismanagement necessarily incident to the operation of the railway by the government.
Now, let us see where that is going to land us. The earnings of the Intercolonial Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
Railway were in round figures $6,000,000. Ordinarily the railways of this country which are operated successfully by railway companies think that they are doing very well if they get 40 per cent of net earnings out of their gross receipts, and putting our earnings at $6,000,000 we would get around to the $2,000,000 basis I spoke of a moment ago, provided our working expenses were one-third of what they ought to be, and provided that this road was being operated under conditions which would apply if a company were operating it, and under which the government is absolutely unable to operate it according to the criticisms which are passed. The working expenses, as you see, were more than would produce that, and they added up to $5,574,000. Where has this money gone to '! I am going to give you a statement showing precisely where these working expenses have gone. I am going to give you the different classes of expenditure, and I think I can give them to you in such a way that you can see clearly the conclusion to which I am pointing, and I think you will agree with the conclusion at which I shall arrive.
First, we have paid $5,574,000 in working expenses. Let us deduct by the process of elimination. The first item that goes to make up that $5,000,000 and upwards is the item of wages, and the item of wages sums up $3,537,000. I have said, and I repeat that the wages of all the employees on the Intercolonial Railway, except those of two or three at the head and except the clerical staff, amount to $233,000, are scheduled and classified, at a rate according to a year after year increase and length of service, and scheduled by agreements which have been arrived at with the different organizations to which the men belong. I say that we do not pay any more than we ought to pay, taking into consideration the present cost of living. We cannot cut them down. You could not attempt to take any portion of this $3,537,000 and point to any of the items and say there is room for economy there, there is waste here, there is extravagance somewhere else. You will have to go into some other fieid if you are going to find wasteful and extravagant expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway under government ownership as compared with corporation railways. You would not find any field in the item of wages in which to operate in the way of making a reduction. If you take $3,500,000 out of $5,500,000 you have only $2,000,000 remaining. Now, you have to get in all your fine work in the way of this political influence within that $2,000,000. Let us see what is the next big item. The next big item is coal. We pay over $1,000,000 for coal. I say we do not pay one dollar more than we are compelled to pay-not one dollar. We ask for public tenders and competition and we buy our coal at the lowest figure we can get it. for. and there are many members of parliament

who know that to be a fact. If we can we take the coal companies by the throat and make them reduce their price, but if we cannot, we have to pay them what they demand. There is no held within the area of the coal item, for exploiting these economical ideas and explaining where political influence, corruption, pressure and wrongdoing hold high carnival. Therefore, you must take off three and a half millions for wages and you must take off another million for coal, and that makes four and a half millions. That leaves you only a million. Now, you will have to find this waste and extravagance within this million. What goes to make up this million ? We pay for printing and advertising $50,000. We may possibly pay a little too much for advertising. We may possibly advertise a little more freely than we ought to, but it is only a mare's nest after all. It does not go very far towards explaining about this $2,000,000. It does not reach out far in that direction. Fifty thousand dollars at all events is paid, and $50,000 will continue to be paid, or in that ratio, and I want to say right here that other railways are just as much subject to the pressure of their friends and outsiders in the way of advertising as the Intercolonial Kailway is. You ask railway men and they will frankly acknowledge it to you. They are not free from this sort of pressure. They want to accommodate their friends, they want to stand well with the public, they want to stand well with the different great corporate bodies and with parliaments, and they show to those people with whom they want to be on friendly terms a good deal of consideration. They are just as subject, just as open to pressure and influence as the Intercolonial Railway or the officers who may be connected with it. Now, we have rentals amounting to $140,000. There is no field for economy there. We pay $67,000 for our ferries and we pay for land damages some $20,000.
We leave, therefore, for general stores and covering the other outlays $750,000. Now if it were all waste; if the whole $750,000 for stores were not required, and we threw it all away, it would still be a long distance from explaining the difference between the 3 per cent, the earnings on capital of the corporation railways, and the results on the Intercolonial Railway. I have an explanation to make with regard to this item for stores. I venture to say that we buy our stores by public tender and by open and public competition to the extent of nine-tenths of the total quantity. I am hazarding a conjecture there, but I think I am not far astray when I say that nine-tenths of our stores are bought in that way. Now I speak with knowledge on the question, and I say that if the railway companies will allow anybody access to their books, who has curiosity enough to inquire, as to how they conduct this department, I will challenge a comparison between what we 115
pay for our stores and what is paid by other railway companies for their stores, and I hold .that the comparison will be favourable to us. People seem always very anxious to supply the government and the competition is exceedingly keen amongst them, and no tendersi are accepted at a higher rate than the lowest offer provided the articles are up to our specifications. I am proud to say that this branch is managed by officers who are most economical and careful men. I do not think it would be possible to find in the service of any of the railway companies, more competent, more careful, more economical and more cautious men than those gentlemen on the Intercolonial Railway to whom the purchasing of these supplies is largely entrusted. There is no field for any considerable reduction in that respect. There will, of course, always be little things come in, but take it from first to last, I do not think there would be a difference of $100,000, even including such things as additional stations which we give for the accommodation of the public more than would be supplied by private railway companies. I say without fear of successful contradiction, that all this talk about the management of the Intercolonial Railway by the government, being wasteful, is a mere bugaboo and will not bear scrutiny.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why does the hon. gentleman not show results then ?

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) will show a little patience I will show him results which will make a favourable impression on his mind, whether he will acknowledge it or not. There is no more efficient test as to whether the government is managing the railway extravagantly or wastefully, or whether it is managing it as economically as other railway companies, than can be found in the sworn returns which according to law are furnished by the railway companies year after year, and which returns are open to inspection by any one who desires to inspect them. Out of curiosity, I have had a careful abstract made of a comparison of the different items on the Intercolonial Railway with the two great railways, the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway. I will give the House the result of that comparison and let the House judge if these figures are not potential in favour of my argument.

Would the hon. gentleman give us the comparison of the earnings per 'train mile ?
I have given it to you.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: You are giving the expenses, I want the earnings.

I am furnishing the hon. member with the return as it is required to be handed in by all the railways according to law. I am not picking -one thing out of one place and another out of another and putting them together. I am giving the return just as it has been brought down.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What I understood the hon. minister to give us was the relative proportion of expenses. I am asking him if he can give the earnings of the Intercolonial Railway per train mile in comparison with those of other railways.

No ; I am just giving you what has been returned. I think the earnings per train mile will be in the same proportion, oi perhaps less than those of other railways. I am not stating that as within my knowledge, but simply as my present judgment warrants me. Now, in view of such statistical and reliable facts as I am presenting, it is a fair conclusion that the Intercolonial Railway has no right to get a black eye, or to be treated in the sneering way in which it is generally spoken of, as a failure, because it does not produce the same net results that other railways do ; and it is unfair to ascribe these consequences in any material degree to political pressure or to government operation. I think that if any gentleman, knowing the conditions that exist on the Intercolonial, were to converse with the managers of any other railway on this subject, they would say that it is a mistake to suppose that the government road is in an exceptional position in that regard, or is more subject to the influences to which reference has been made. I had a conversation with a prominent railway man, a president of one of the railways in the United States, only a few months ago, and in the course of the conversation I opened up this subject. I told him that the government railway was rather prejudiced in the minds of the people because it was said : You cannot resist pressure, and that must always be detrimental to the management of a government railway. He said:	'I do not
know to what extent pressure of that kind exists in your country, but I can tell you that we in the United States are not by any means free from it. Although we are operating a company railway, we are subject to it. Do not run away with the impression

that corporation railways are exempt from such disabilities ; they exist with respect to them just as you say it is alleged they exist with respect to your government railway.'
Now, the earnings and working expense's of the Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific Railway for the year ending the 30th of June last were as follows

Net earnings	$ 7,814,120 99 $14,043,674 75
If we were to earn a couple of million dollars in excess of our working expenses, our showing would be relatively as good as theirs. Well, I am going to come down to the kernel of this matter, and I am going to show you why we do not earn that much. I am going to show you that the fault does not lie in the management of the road, nor in the fact that it is owned by the government. The fact is not due to any wastefulness, extravagance or wrong-doing of any kind, nor to any causes that are not incidental to other railways as well as government railways. There are two causes. One is a greater cause than the other. I will refer to the minor cause first, though it is not very much inferior to the other. The minor cause is the location of the railway. There is no question that the Intercolonial was not located with reference to business or commercial considerations. I have remarked before, and I remark now, that there was one particular in which political considerations did fatally injure the Intercolonial Railway. That injury was done, not merely once, but for the entire life of the railway. The location of the Intercolonial was most unhappy from the point of view of achieving financial results, and was due entirely to those considerations of state-imperial, if you will-war considerations, large and potent considerations, which were thought to overbalance altogether business considerations. As everybody knows, the location is very unfavourable, not only because of the enormous distances between important points and between the termini of the railway, but because of the inferior character, from a productive business point of view, of a large portion of the country which it traverses. A large portion of the railway does not yield returns at all commensurate with the cost of its operation. That important portion between St. John and Halifax is, I think, paying quite a handsome return over its cost and the expenses of operation ; but the rest of the railway is not, and that is due to the enormous distances over which the traffic has to be hauled, to the small amount of local traffic which comes to the road, and to another consideration of a very potent character, which is, that at almost every important point on the road, at all events from 115J
Halifax nearly to Montreal, it has to face water competition. The Intercolonial Railway has settled land only on one side of it; it has water on the other side. It is a onesided institution in that respect, and it suffers under that disability.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: And the Canadian Pacific Railway on the other side.

Yes, and the Canadian Pacific Railway on the other side. But that is not all. That disability cannot be removed. I doubt if the other can be removed. I had a careful study made and a careful statement furnished to me by the traffic officers of the Intercolonial Railway, as to the general traffic, of tolls and freight charges which govern on the Intercolonial Railway and those which govern on the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway; and the result of that statement, keeping-well on the safe side, is that the rates upon those two railways are from fifty to one hundred per cent higher than those upon the Intercolonial Railway. I am not going to suggest that the rates upon either of the two other roads are higher than they ought to be. I have not the requisite knowledge which would enable me to pass an opinion. But I do know that the rates on the Intercolonial Railway are even lower than I have stated, when you consider the question of distances and the question of scarcity of traffic. It goes without saying that it costs no more money to carry a thousand tons of freight at $10 than at $5 per ton. If then you add fifty per cent, which is the minimum excess of the rates of freights on the other roads as compared with the Intercolonial Railway, to the earnings of the Intercolonial Railway in the carriage of freight, our revenue would be increased by that amount and our expenditure would not be increased one farthing. Let me make a calculation. The gross earnings of the Intercolonial Railway on its traffic, not including passenger traffic, for the year 1902 were $3,900,000. Add fifty per cent to that to bring it up to this minimum excess, and you get $1,950,000 of addition. In other words, if we could have collected on the Intercolonial Railway the minimum rates charged by other railways, we would have had $1,950,000 more revenue from freight than we did, and this would have brought our total earnings up to $7,600,000, including passenger traffic. And our working expenses would not have been increased. Deducting working expenses, we would have had a surplus for 1902 of $2,046,000. My hon. friend smiles, but these figures cannot be gainsaid.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I smile when I think of what we have missed by not putting up the rates.

I would smile on the other side

of my face if I were asked to put up the rates. We have no right to put up the rates. Nobody expejcts it. If my hon. friend were in charge, he would not put them up, or if he did, he would take them down again. We cannot put them up. The rates on the Intercolonial Railway are no higher than those which were imposed at the time when part of it was owned and operated by the government of Nova Scotia and another part by the government of New Brunswick. The rates are, I think, substantially the same. When confederation was formed, the Dominion took over the road under the conditions and rates then existing, and from that time down the people of this country, the government and parliament, have all agreed that these rates and conditions should continue, and they exist to-day. Another reason why it would not be possible to raise the rates to any appreciable extent is to be found in the fact that the Intercolonial Railway is subjected at every point to a keen and active water competition. If you were to raise the rates, you would find that you would not get the business. I repeat that we would have $2,000,000 better results if we were to be treated upon even less than the present basis upon which the other two systems are conducting their business. This is a material and fair argument, because those who condemn the management of the Intercolonial Railway do not condemn it because it does not put up its rates. They do not look at that side of the account. They condemn it on account of wastefulness and extravagance and wrong-doings which they never specify and cannot indicate, and because the financial results do not make any kind of comparison with those of the other great railways. You have therefore $2,046,000 which would have gone into the treasury of this country if the rates on freights had been fifty per cent higher than were charged last year. That would have shown forty per cent earnings to sixty per cent working expenses, and everybody would have exclaimed ' what marvellously good management and administration.' You can always furnish evidence of that. All you have to do is tax the people a little heavier, make them pay a little more if possible, and you have this evidence of splendid administration. $2,046,000 would have paid three per cent nearly on the whole cost of the Intercolonial Railway, which is just as good as either of these other companies are doing. Take the rates in the Australian colonies, and you will find that they are a good deal higher than the rates on which I based my argument.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Higher than our rates with fifty per cent added ?

Yes, higher than the minimum excess over ours. $2,000,000 might have been brought into the treasury if we could have Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
added fifty per cent to our rates, but that money remained in the pockets of the people who have done business over the Intercolonial Railway. They have been taxed that much less, and if the Intercolonial Railway has relieved these people of $2,000,000 taxes and contributed besides in a material degree to the general improvement of business and the development of the country, I am not so sure that the people have not reaped as good results as if that money had gone into the treasury. So beneficial are these results that if the people were thoroughly cognizant of the advantages which have accrued to them from using the Intercolonial Railway- and these advantages are not confined to any one province by any means-they would never cavil at the results. And they would only wish that it had occurred to somebody in times past to construct a railway through their portion of the country instead of aiding to build railways to be owned and managed by private corporations. In making this defence of the Intercolonial management I appeal to the judgment and opinion of those who do business with the road, and I am sure that they will say that they are well satisfied with the manner in which they have been served and that they would be truly sorry if any change were made under which the tolls were changed so as to lay an additional burden on the traflic that is carried.
Now, Sir, I have pointed out these advantages, and I will here endeavour to give to the House a thorough and complete statement of the actual existing conditions. I do not know that, as respects this question of rates and tolls upon the road, the people of Canada have been as fully informed before as I have now informed them. I do not think there is any disadvantage in the people knowing these facts ; I think they are entitled to be apprised of them. And I believe that when they realize all that has been done by the government railroad in the development of these portions of Canada, and the increase of traffic with the other provinces, that the connection it affords has brought about, and when they realize that ail this has been done at such a moderate cost to the country and has imposed so light a burden upon the people, I think they will realize as they have not realized before the magnificent property they possess in the Intercolonial Railway of Canada. I do not think they realize it now, but I hope they will come to that realization.
I am not making, I hope, any personal or individual claim in regard to these results. Only in a very small measure should I be entitled to do so. If I were to award credit for the showing we are able to make, I would award the greatest sjiare to the good men and true, faithful in their duty and loyal to the public, who give their best attention and employ their best energies in the discharge of the duties connected with the Intercolonial service. I think they

are entitled to great credit, indeed, I venture to say tlmt you cannot travel over any railway in Canada on which you will find a better class of men, more attentive, more courteous, or are more deeply interested in their work and in the welfare of the road they serve. 1 am bound to say this in justice to the employees of the road, for so I have heard them spoken of by many who have travelled over the Intercolonial Railway. To these men I would award their proper measure of praise. I am only claiming for the government that we realized what the necessities of the hour demanded, we realized what would be desirable-nay, what would be imperative-if we would rescue the Intercolonial Railway from the alarming condition in which it was ; if we .were to escape a continuance not merely of half million deficits, but of deficits far in excess of half a million ; realized that it was necessary that we should go to work in a business like way, that we should adopt modern methods, that we should act as men who knew that good results were to be achieved only by adopting the means necessary for the economical working of the railway and the carrying of its traffic. It was only because we were impressed with the importance and necessity of going about the working of the Intercolonial Railway from that point of view that I claim we are entitled to credit from the people of this country.

The Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) began his statement concerning the affairs of the Intercolonial Railway with a comparison between the management of the present day and the management of 1896 under my regime. He made a comparison of the sums spent on maintenance out of revenue account last year and in 1896 which appears very favourable to his own administration. I could not take down all the items, but I shall have an opportunity later on of examining them, and, perhaps, of discussing them more in detail than it is possible for me to do just now. Fancy the minister charged with the management of the Intercolonial Railway, having nearly double the locomotive power and car accommodation that his predecessors had, claiming the extra amount expended in repairs to locomotives, tanks, cars and so on, as an extra sum spent in improving the road and enabling him to compare his management favourably with that of his predecessor. Then he goes on to say that the higher rates of wages paid to keep the road in repair makes a certain aggregate sum over that spent in 1896, and, assuming that the same amount of work is done per day by each man, the whole is to be counted as
paid for the improvement of the road and is iu favour of the management of the present day in comparison with that of 1896. The whole comparison is about as absurd a one as it is possible for a minister of the Crown to make. Because he spent $500,000 more than his predecessors in repairs to passenger cars, stations, roadbed, and so on, he claims this whole amount as an improvement of the road and a benefit to the country, and so much in his favour as compared with his predecessor. The whole thing was simply a part of the hon. gentleman's advocacy of the idea of the government road being extended from the present terminus perhaps of Georgian bay, perhaps to the prairies of the west, perhaps to the Pacific coast. I hear many supporters of the hon. gentleman voicing that opinion. But, before I am done, 1 think that if they are ready to take the Intercolonial Railway under its present auspices as a basis of judgment as to this proposition, they will hardly be so favourably impressed with it. Let me show what the hon. gentleman has expended oil the road since he got into power, in 1897. I gave the figures a couple of years ago, but I would like to put them again before the country. If the country can calmly contemplate such an alarming expenditure-I am not going to say extravagant expenditure-on one of its important works as that which was made for the purpose of having the Intercolonial road extended to a terminus in the city of Montreal, and if they submit to it without complaint, it is their fault and not ours. Our duty is simply to draw the people's attention to the enormous expenditure which is being made by the hon. gentleman in the management of the Intercolonial Railway. speechtext: Then I am obliged to go to the estimates. I will give as nearly as possible the expenditure for the year. The amount voted for the Intercolonial for 1902-3 was $3,200,000, of which I see, appropriation not required, $978,800. I am debiting tbe minister only with what he has expended of that amount. It is possible that in the supplementary estimates a provision will have to be made for an expenditure during the year further than what is stated in these estimates, and I am pretty certain there will. However, the amount would be $2,281,200 that was expended on capital account last year. He has expended on the Prince Edward Island Railway, on capital account, $2,736,200, that is, adding the deficits from 1897 up to the present year.
Does the hon. gentleman complain of that expenditure ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I am simply making a statement of the expenditure the hon. gentleman has made on railways. The hon. gentleman interrupted me a while ago, and he said that what I was saying did not affect the argument. What pertinence has it to the argument whether I object to tbe expenditure or not ? The amount expended, then, is $2,736,200. But there is besides a large amount, I see, to be added to the capital account in the current year, there is a large amount asked for the Intercolonial and a large amount for the Prince Edward Island Railway. We pay to the Grand Trunk Railway a certain sum every year, $140,000. Deducting the $140,000, which the hon. gentleman has a right to take to his credit the amount capitalized at 3 per cent which has been paid out of the revenue of the Intercolonial for the present year, is $4,526,607. So there was actually expended in cash, $18,798,670, or adding these two amounts together, $23,325,331, from 1897 down to the first of June next. Supposing, Sir, we had a government railway stretching from Montreal across to the Pacific, and supposing it was under the management of the Minister of Railways, what would be the amount expended in five years on capital expenditure on that road ? What position would the country be in with a like expenditure as upon the Intercolonial ? The hon. minister may talk, but these are the bald, naked facts that stick out to view. They came into possession of the Intercolonial Railway with a capital account of a little less than $44,000,000, and at the present day it is nearly $69,000,000. The hon. gentleman talks about the improvements he has made to the road and he says that the amount of rolling stock and the number of locomotives that he found upon the road when he took possession were not sufficient

for the working' of the road. I have from his deputy who sits heside him here, his trusted and efficient man, and from the manager of his road down there of whom he speaks so favourably, a statement that there were more than sufficient locomotives and rolling stock for the Intercolonial Railway and that if I acquired the Drummond County Railway, there was sufficient to run it without purchasing more rolling stock. The hon. gentleman says :	Look how efficient the
Intercolonial Railway is. The balance of mileage instead of being against us to the extent of $80,000, is now $15,000 in our favour. Does the hon. minister know the effect of the statement he is making ? What is the reason ? Simply this; that it is notorious in every part of the country that he has a superabundance of rolling stock, and that it is being used by every railway in every section of the country. That is the cause of the balance being the other way. I put a notice upon' the paper in regard to that question, because I had heard that no railway down near the Intercolonial Railway purchases rolling stock at all. They rely upon running their roads with the locomotives of the Intercolonial Railway. The Canadian Pacific Railway borrowed eight locomotives from the hon. gentleman. Nearly all the passenger coaches and freight cars used by the different roads in that section of the country belong to the Intercolonial Railway, and then the hon. minister gets up and boasts of the balance of mileage being in his favour to the extent of $15,000 a year.
