Mr. Speaker, before six o'clock I was dealing with the comparison which the Minister of Railways had made between the expenditure for maintenance upon the Intercolonial Railway in 1902, as compared with the expenditure under my administration in 1896. He spoke of the increased rate of wages at the present day compared with what it was in 1896, but it never seemed to have occurred to the Minister of Railways that if a man did the same work in 1896 that he did in 1902, the increase in wages would be an argument to the minister's disadvantage, because if the rate of wages is $1.25 now and I paid $1 a day in 1896, then if the same man did the same day's work I got for $1 what the Minister of Railways is expending $1.25 for. I do not wish to use any term which might be considered in any way opprobrious, but I think I may say that to my mind the argument of the Minister of Railways is an absurdity. Before six o'clock I spoke of the enormous expenditure which the people of this country were called on to make, a sum
of about $23,000,000, for the purpose of extending the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal. Why, Sir, that amounts to nearly the whole surplus of this country in the time of its prosperity, and it could have been better spent in works of utility which would have been beneficial to Canada. We could have had a government railway, if necessary, from the province of Ontario to the prairie lands of the North-west for nearly the same sum of money which the hon. gentleman has expended in improvements on the Intercolonial Railway. I have no objection to improvements on the Intercolonial Railway, providing the expenditure is used for the advantage of Canada, but the position of the Intercolonial Railway to-day is no better than it was in 1896. It may have increased accommodation and a good many things that way ; it may have better cars, but the road in 1896 was one of the best roads on the continent of America, so far as roadbed is concerned. My instruction to my officers of the department was to keep up the rolling stock to the fullest extent, so as to make the Intercolonial Railway of the highest standard amongst all the railroads on the continent of America. And it was, too. It had rolling stock sufficient for its purpose. When the hon. gentleman came into power he made the statement that the expenditure he would make on the Drummond County to extend the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal would be repaid to the people of the country tlmough the benefits that would be derived from the increased business of the Intercolonial Railway. But the hon. gentleman has a new system of book-keeping. The Intercolonial Railway is in a different category from any other railway in the country in that respect. Other railroads have to pay interest on their bonds and other securities, but the anomaly and paradox in reference to the Intercolonial Railway is that it is government money that is going into it, and it is not expected to pay interest at all on the investment that the country makes in it. We are not only to keep the promise that we made with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick at the time of confederation, but we are to go on with interminable expenditures until the capital account in that road alone is $68,000,090, and it is not expected that the country is to be recouped in any way for that expenditure. It is to be for the benefit of the people down there, in cheaper freights, in the cheaper carrying of passengers, and it is all done without any political bias or political influence at all.
Hear, hear.
I am glad to hear that the Minister of Railways states that no political influence enters into the administration of the Intercolonial Railway.

Oh.
Other hon. MEMBERS. Hear, hear.

It was so in my day.
Some lion. MEMBERS. Oh.

Yes ; it was so in my day, and the hon. gentleman says it is so in his day. It is possible, however, that on some great occasions tickets may have been given under his regime to electors for the purpose of enabling them to reach the polls to vote in the right direction.
In consequence of the lights in the Chamber having gone out, Mr. Speaker -announced that the sitting of the House would be suspended for half an hour.
House resumed at 8.55.

Mr. Speaker, when the lights went out, I was speaking about the protest of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals against the suggestion that any political influence was exercised in the control of the Intercolonial Railway. He assured the House that no political influence was allowed to interfere with it in any manner, which he intimated was in strong contrast with the management of the railway under his predecessors. Well, if the bon. gentleman does not use political influence in connection with the Intercolonial Railway, he has changed his mind since a short time after he became Minister of Railways and Canals. In the town in which 1 reside there were two bridge tenders employed, and when the. hon. gentleman came into power he dismissed these men without a single complaint being,niade against either of them, and appointed political supporters of his in their places. In addition to that, he sent a letter to Mr. Frost, at present a senator, who was at the time representing Reeds and Grenville, stating that there were fifteen employees on the Rideau canal-a good many of them were old sergeants, some of whom had been in the British service for twenty years or more-and asking the hon. gentleman to recommend successors to these men. Mr. Frost stated in this House that he had received that letter ; but he bad enough honour in his composition not to accept the proposition of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals, and lie refused to name any successors to them. This is the hon. gentleman who declares to this House and the country at large that no political influence is being used in connection with the Intercolonial Railway. He has changed his mind and his method since he came into power, and it is a good thing for his party that he has done so, after that slap in the face which he got from one of his strongest supporters in this House. What has become of the hon. gentleman's promise ? He asked and obtained from this country over .$18,000,000 in cash for the purpose of extending the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal, besides an amount which capitalized would equal $4,000,000, making altogether $22,000,000. He gave authority to the right hon. gentleman who leads the Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
House to make the statement in Soluner Park, Montreal, that the Intercolonial Railway would recoup to the people of Canada the extra expenditure that was incurred in extending the railway to Montreal, and that the era of deficits would cease. How has he performed that promise ? He comes here to-day and claims a nominal surplus of $96,000. How does he arrive at that surplus? By charging to capital account items which ought to be and which formerly were charged to the ordinary revenue of the Intercolonial Railway. He comes here with a statement which does not compare with those of his predecessors, because his system of book-keeping is entirely different. He does this notwithstanding the fact that the leaders of the Reform party in the House claimed again and again that it was time that the capital account of the Intercolonial Railway was changed. So it is ; it is time the people of Canada knew the difference between cooked balances on the Intercolonial Railway and the real loss that the running of that railway imposes upon them. The real loss to the country from 1867 up to the present time in the running of the Intercolonial Railway is $23,000,000, and the railway is the better 1o the extent of the extra rolling stock that it has, the Drummond Counties Railway, and the terminal facilities in Montreal. The hon. Minister of Railways has done more to prevent the people of this country embarking in a government railway than any other man. He has pointed out what the result would be if the Intercolonial Railway were extended to the Pacific ocean. What would be the result if the charges to capital account on such a railway were in the same proportion as those he has made on the Intercolonial Railway ? The whole revenues of this country, I will venture to say, would not supply the deficits of such a railroad conducted in the same manner as the Intercolonial Railway. The hon. gentleman states perfectly correctly that the government can obtain employees for a government railway as cheaply as any corporation in Canada. He states also, what is true, that the supplies for such a road could be got as cheaply by the government as by any private corporation.
Except ties.

the small roads in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick-which would not rather give the hon. gentleman his $15,000 balance in his favour in order to utilize his rolling stock ?
Let me point out further that the increased receipts on the Intercolonial Railway are due to the increased local trade in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia. The results attained by building the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal have not fulfilled one-fiftieth part of the hon. gentleman's expectation. Where does he get his increased freight from ? He gets it through the increased development of Nova Scotia 'and New Brunswick, his own province, but the doubling of the amount carried of one single article-lumber. The hon. gentleman states that he has had to contend with enormous difficulties in getting his surplus of $96,000; he has to pay so much more for labour, so much for supplies, so much more for coal. Why does he not start a coal mine of his own ? I know the difficulty the hon. gentleman hast to contend with-a combine amongst the coal mine owners of Nova Scotia. I had to contend with the same. They fix the price and divide the quantity to be furnished the Intercolonial Railway according to the output of the several companies, and they-
The hon. gentleman (Hon. Mr. Haggart) never paid over $2.10 a ton.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
That may be. But I had to pay more than the Canadian Pacific or the Grand Trunk for the same coal. The hon. gentleman has virtually told us that he pays for coal far more than he ought to pay. He and his department simply do not use sufficient means to get the product of the mines delivered to the road at reasonable prices. If I remember rightly, we paid nearly $2 per ton at the pit's mouth, which is nearly double the price it ought to be, and I think the hon. minister pays nearly $3. Of course, that helps to account for the large expenditure on the Intercolonial. I have just said that the hon. gentleman has had the benefit of the development in the maritime provinces which did not exist in 1896. And what is the cause of that development ? The cause is the policy of his predecessors, the building up of manufacturing industries and the expansion of the steel and iron manufacturers as well as the increased production of coal resulting from the duty preventing competition from abroad. We started all this development which has reached its climax in Cape Breton and which has given the hon. gentleman as he tells us, the best paying branch of the road's business, carrying freight and passengers between Halifax and Cape Breton. Besides that, the hon. gentleman has had advantages which he shares with every other road on the continent of America. This has been a growing time. There has been abundance Hon. Mr. HAGGART.
all over the continent. There is enormously increased passenger traffic and freight traffic as well-far in excess of any time with which the hon. gentleman makes a comparison. He has advantages of the best times which this country has ever known. Andi what is the result ? By an expenditure of at least $2,000,000 which he ought fairly to have charged to revenue account, he is able to come down with a surplus of barely $96,000. Is this carrying out the promise to the people that he would put life into the old road ? Is this carrying out what he told us when he said that expenditures such as these he was making were like those of a man moving from a back street to a main street, and spending money to increase his business-that the increased expenditure would justify itself by increased revenue ? After all this enormous outlay at the expense of the country, he comes before us with a nominal surplus of $96,000, a surplus which can be manipulated at any time by those who have control of the financial statements of the Intercolonial to show a deficit or a surplus according to the wishes perhaps of the officers of the department, or even of the head of the department himself. The hon. gentleman need not make comparison with 1896, for as I have said, times are different. My expenditure on capital account for the six years in which I had charge of the road, including loss on working, did not amount to one-third of that under the hon. gentleman.
I have spoken longer than I intended to speak at this time. I shall have an opportunity to go into details when the estimates are before us. The information which I expect and hope to get at that time will enable me intelligently to discuss these details. There are other gentlemen in this House who are more fully conversant with these things than I am. But the bold, hard fact sticks out, and meets the view of the most casual observer, that in his management for the last six years the hon. gentleman has shown nothing but an absolute increase of debt upon the road of nearly $18,000,000 in cash, besides $4,000,000 of an obligation to the Grand Trunk. Yet we have heard the hon. gentleman speak in many parts of this country in advocacy of government railways and of further expenditure for that purpose by the people of this country. This, to my mind, is too ridiculous. He may get some of his friends who have no other politics, but further expenditure in the provinces which they represent to approve his policy. But we have a different and higher view. We are in favour of the advancement of this country and are ready to advocate the expenditure of any sums necessary for the development of the country as a whole; but we are not ready to fling further enormous sums into the sink hole that he has made of the Intercolonial I Rajlway to-day.

I had not intended to say anything on this subject to-night, expecting, at a later stage, to go into the hon. minister's (Hon. Mr. Blair's) figures in some detail. But, as the hon. minister has made a rather pointed allusion to myself, or rather to the criticisms which I made upon his accounts last year, and the year before, X think I may be permitted to say a few words now in reply to his general observations. The hon. gentleman, perhaps, does not himself need that I should say one word in answer to the argument which he has made this afternoon. But his remarks seemed to meet with so much applause from hon. gentlemen behind him, that I may be excused if I say a few words to show how utterly fallacious is his argument in making, or appearing to make, a comparison between the operation of the government railway and that of other Canadian railways. I do not think I need occupy much time in showing that, but I think I can show it rather effectively. The hon. gentleman is perfectly aware-I have pointed it out to him before this-that the system on which he keeps his accounts is one which prevents the people from making any attempt to compare his operations and the percentage of his working expenses with those of other railways. I pointed that out more than once, and the hon. gentleman is as well aware of it as I am myself or as any person can possibly be. But, before X take up a few of the items in which the hon. gentleman so far departs from the ordinary system of keeping accounts, I wish to point out the results of the hon. gentleman's operations as he has shown them himself. Iu his report-and I have taken the few figures I have here entirely from his own report-he shows that the gross earnings of all the railways of this country during the year for which this report was made up, amounted to $83,666,502. He shows that the working expenses of all these railways, including the government railways, amounted to $57,343,592. Now, in order to ascertain exactly what the working expenses of the other railways are, apart from the government railways, I deduct his own working expenses and earnings, and the result shows that all the railways outside the government railways have earned during the year $77,747,513, and their working expenses were $53,482,494. Now, Sir, the result of that is that all the railways of Canada, big and little, in new districts and old districts, taking all their operations, earnings and expenses, have on the average worked at sixty-six and one-fifth per cent, while the government railways-I am including the Intercolonial and the Prince Edward Island Railway-the operation of which the hon. gentleman is so proud of. were worked at, what do you think, Mr. Speaker ? Ninety-nine per cent. The hon. gentleman earns for this country $1 for every $100 that he takes
in. The result of the operations of the two raliways is, even according to his own statement, and omitting hundreds of thousands of dollars that ought to be charged to working expenses, the result that the hon. gentleman has giveu us as something that he is entitled to be proud of, is $57,891, or a little less than about one-thirteenth of one per cent upon the capital invested ; and this Js the wonderful result that was applauded by hon. gentlemen opposite.
Now, it may be quite true as the hon. geu-tleman says, that his traffic is worked at a lower rate than the traffic on other railways.
I do not accept unreservedly the hon. gentleman's figures in this respect ; though I wdl do so for the moment; but it does strike me that it is a most extraordinary statement- and I presume the hon. gentleman was speaking on behalf of the government that we should hear from the government that this railway is worked at such rates that there are $2,000,000 lost every year in railway operation in order that a section of the country should get low rates at the expense of the entire community. I do not know whether that will be a pleasing thing for hon. gentlemen to announce to their constiu-ents ; I should say that it was a most extraordinary statement. The hon. gentleman tells us that the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway have certain rates that he says are not unreasonable, and that if he charged those rates upon the railway under his administration he would have earned $2,000,000 more, and he would have had that surplus. Yet the hon. gentleman, having an opportunity to thus .earn $2,000,000 a year, and save something of the many millions he has been expending during the last six or seven years on capital account, prefers to take that money out of the public funds of this country and let the people in the eastern provinces get ahead of the rest of the Dominion by just so much per annum. That is the result of the hon. gentleman s statement.
Now, I hope it is not quite so bad as that. I think perhaps the hon. gentleman has occasionally been carrying freight to St. John, where he has been spending so much money in recent years, at less than cost. I think tlyit is very probable, but I doubt whether the hon. gentleman is carrying all his traffic at these wonderfully low rates. All I can say is that if he has, the rest of this Dominion have got something to say in the matter. We surely have a right to contend that the business on that government railway should be so conducted that if $2,000,000, or $1,000,000, or $500,000, can be earned at reasonable rates, that money should be earned, and the capital expenditure the hon. gentleman is making year by year should be reduced accordingly. Surely that is a plain business proposition.
But I want to show that the hon. gen-tlaman'.s working expenses are not the working expenses as they are understood by

all ordinary railway companies. And before I show that I want to point out that the hon. gentleman's working expenses as they are in his accounts to-day are not at all those of his predecessor, they do not mean the same thing at all. The hon. gentleman's predecessor charged to working expenses many things that the hon. gentleman is now paying out of capital account.
I beg your pardon.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I beg your pardon also. I am speaking of that which I know, and I can say this, that not only is the hon. gentleman charging differently from what his predecessor charged, but he is charging differently from what he himself charged the first couple of years of his administration. The hon. gentleman got new light as lie went on. His predecessor, when he put in new rails on the government railways to replace old rails worn out in service, charged the whole cost to working expenses. The hon. gentleman knows that, he cannot dispute it, his officers will tell him that is so. Not only that, but when his predecessor put in heavier rails he charged the whole cost, even of the additional weight of metal to his working expenses. He was not obliged to do so, it was against himself. When the hon. gentleman began his operations in 1807 he followed the very same course that his predecessor did. But since then, what has the hon. gentleman done ? Why, he takes up the sixty-seven pound rail that was there before, which was worn out by use, and which it was his duty to replace by another sixty-seven pound rail at the cost of his working expenses, and he puts in a new oigfity pound rail. He would be entitled to charge only thirteen pounds, but he charges the whole eighty pounds to capital. I showed that last year and the year before, I gave the figures, I worked it all out on the figures in the hon. gentleman's own report. I showed that the hon. gentleman had charged to capital $436,000 for steel rails, every dollar of which ought to have gone to working expenses. I have not made up the figures in his report for this year to see exactly what amount the hon. gentleman ought to have charged against revenue that he has - charged to capital. But taking the same proportion as in the previous year the hon. gentleman ought now to add about $400,000 for rails to his present working expenses. The hon. gentleman for this year 1901-2 obtained a vote of $600,000 for rails. I have not gone through the accounts closely enough yet to see exactly how much he expended, but he got that appropriation on capital account, and he insisted that he had a right to charge that to capital. It was protested against last year and the year before. The hon. gentleman did not answer the argument but he stuck to his flag and insisted upon getting money on capital account. If the same

proportion has been expended there will be $400,000 which should have gone to his working expenses and the $57,000 that he claims as a surplus, does not exist at all. He has a deficit instead of a surplus. I should say here that last year we had Mr. Pottinger, the general manager of the railway, in the witness box before a committee of this House andj I put a question to Mr. Pottinger, as the hon. minister will recollect. I said, Mr. Pottinger, do you as a railway man piretend that you are justified in charging the w'hole cost of these new rails, replacing old rails, to capital account ? The hon. minister knows what Mr. Pottinger's answer was. I quoted it last year and I will quote it again from Hansard. I asked Mr. Pottinger what he thought of charging to capital account all the cost of replacing rails. Mr. Pottinger's answer I quoted then and I quote it again.
Why should I object so long as parliament votes the money ?
That was the reply of the hon. gentleman's chief official whom he lauds here tonight. Why should these railway officials object to parliament voting them money for capital expenditure that they ought to charge to working expenses ? No railway official would object to that. Mr. Pottinger from,his answer never pretended that this was a proper way of charging the money. He never pretended that any other railway company would charge it in that way. Mr. Pottinger admitted inferentially that it was an improper charge, that he had no right to charge it to capital when he said : Why should I object when parliament votes the money ? What could more clearly show that the hon. gentleman is improperly charging to capital what he ought to charge to working expenses ? He is by his method misrepresenting to this House the true state of the account and the true result of the operations of the railway.
There is another feature of the hon. gentleman's accounts that I pointed out last year, and it appears again this year, but in an exaggerated form. I pointed out last year that the hon. gentleman was buying rolling stock, buying cars on capital account that he ought to provide out of working expenses. He had a large number of old cars on hand condemned as unfit for traffic. The hon. gentleman's duty, as would be the duty of any railway manager, as any railway manager acting for an ordinary company would be compelled to do, was to replace these cars out of his working expenses and he should not have been allowed to charge one car, one dollar on capital account, until he had replaced every car that had been worn out in the service, out of his expense account. What did he do last year ? The hon. gentleman had 364 cars, I think, condemned. These cars would have cost him to replace out of his working expenses, $250,000. But the hon. gentleman did not charge them to working expenses.

He just left them as condemned cars and used capital from parliament to enable him to substitute others for them ; and they are there in the condemned list still. I will show that from the report which the hon. gentleman has just issued. The hon. gentleman started his year on the 1st July last with 364 condemned cars. These are the ones that last year I said it was his business to replace out of working expenses before he bought new cars out of capital. The hon. gentleman has had condemned during the year 272 more cars, making a total of 636 condemned cars. He has rebuilt only sixty-one, leaving 575 condemned cars in his stock to-day. Of course, as the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) says, he could not be lending cars to the railways in the neighbourhood at twenty-five cents a day if he had 575 dead cars and did not replace them. What did the hon. gentleman do ? It is all here in his report. He purchased during the year on capital account 1,342 new cars. No wonder the hon. gentleman does not do his repairs, and it is not much wonder that he can show $57,000 profit on the operation of the road. If the Grand Trunk Railway and Canadian Pacific Railway would only manage their accounts in that way they could pay very rosy dividends to their stockholders. I think the Grand Trunk Railway would be able to pay dividends on Its common stock. The hon. gentleman has a simple method, he gets a vote in parliament. The hon. gentleman obtained a vote of $2,000,000 for rolling stock on capital account. He provided 1,342 cars out of capital, and he has 575 cars, lying there condemned and out of service. It is the simplest kind of book-keeping in the world. If the hon. gentleman was subject to an auditor acting for shareholders against officials, that auditor would have told the hon. gentleman that 767 of these 1,342 cars should be charged to capital and 575 to working expenses. The hon. gentleman knows that perfectly well. I suppose it is one of the elementary principles that a going concern must maintain its property out of revenue and not out of capital ; and the hon. gentleman has never made a pretense of showing to this House any justification for this sort of thing that has been going on year after year. The hon. gentleman thought he had me in a corner when he asked on a previous occasion : Did you look into the state of the rolling stock when I took it over ? I told him I did and I gave the status of the rolling stock as handed over to him by his predecessor ; and there was a very small number of cars at the time out of service. I pointed out to the minister year after year he had gone on increasing in a very large degree the number of dead stock on his hands and that all the time he had been adding to the rolling stock out of capital account. When the hon. gentleman boasts, as he did boast a few hours ago, of what he had been doing
and when he said that he had not been borrowing money, that lie had been doing all these things out of the results of the operation of the road, the hon. gentleman must have overlooked his charges to capital for cars and steel rails. The hon. gentleman has added about $20,000,000 to the debt of the country since he has been operating this road. In seven years he has put nearly $12,000,000 on the Intercolonial Railway proper and yet the hon. gentleman thinks he is not borrowing anything while operating the road. He reminds me very much of that gentleman in Dickens who, when he gave a promissory note, said : Thank Heaven that is paid. The hon. gentleman thinks when he has expended money on capital account he has not borrowed it, that it has fallen from the clouds. Anything he can stick into capital account just helps to make so much apparent profit in his operations and so much more applause from the hon. gentlemen behind him. Then the hon. gentleman speaks about the economy with which he is buying his stores. Well, I think he must have a wonderful opinion of the short memories of the hon. gentleman behind him. Has the hon. Minister of Railways utterly forgotten what appeared last year in the reports of his own officers about the purchase of those 1,300,000 ties ? The hon. gentleman did not require to put in more than 500,000 ties in any year, and yet in that wonderful season, when the general election was on, he bought 1,300,000 ties, and, according to the reports of his own officials, many of those ties had only four inches face, and were more like scantlings than railway ties. That is his economy ; that is the wonderful management that the hon. gentleman claims credit for. I will say this for his officials, that they ferreted this thing out. The manager-I do not know whether it is the gentleman who has just left the service or not-that gentleman insisted on an inquiry, but it does not appear from first to last that the minister was very active in the investigation. The manager insisted upon the inquiry, and up to a certain point it was carried out at the instance of the official, but if it had not been for that inquiry made, we perhaps would have never have heard of this thing at all. All we do know about the minister's part in it is that at one stage of the proceedings he gave a certain pencil order to one of the contractors. So far as that inquiry did go it disclosed a most disgraceful state of affairs in purchases on the Intercolonial Railway. The minister gave us some details about train mileage and other matters of that kind, which I shall take the opportunity of going into in more detail on another occasion. I will only say now. that the minister knows as well as I do that cost per train mile depends to some extent ppon whether the train mileage is excessive ; whether he isi running fewer cars or lighter trains, or more frequent trains, than would be run by any ordinary manager,
Hear, hear.

I only want to make one more remark. I do not know myself about the hiring of cars to other companies. The hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) says they are hired at 25 cents a day. I can only say this, Mr. Speaker : that if railway companies can hire freight cars at 25 cents a day, no company in this country is very likely to be so foolish as to buy cars while the minister will supply them at that rate. Surely it must be a mistake. It seems to be absurd. It means simply that a railway car lent out by this government is supposed to run from twenty to twenty-five miles a day. I hope that the hon. gentleman will be able to contradict the statement because if he is hiring these cars, and we can only get that rate out of them, the sooner we get out of the business the better.

After the able criticism on the present management of the Intercolonial Railway, which was delivered by the hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) and by the hon. member for Hamilton (Mi-. Barker), it is unnecessary for me to take up the time of the

House at any length. However, Sir, there was a statement made by the minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) which is so contrary to the real facts of the case-facts that are within my own intimate knowledge and within the intimate knowledge of every person in the province of New Brunswick at least-that I must raise my voice in protest against that statement. I refer to his statement with respect to non-interference on the part of officers of the department and on the part of himself with the franchise of the employees of the road. Never in the history of the Intercolonial Railway has there been so much interference with the franchise of its employees as there has been under the management of the present minister. Why, Sir, not content with interfering with the right of the men to vote as they please in federal elections (for which there might be some excuse on the ground of political exigencies), the minister has interfered with their freedom of voting in provincial elections, a thing that was never known of until he took charge of that department. He, or his satellites, has gone so far as even to interfere with the men voting in municipal elections. We had a provincial election in New Brunswick only a few months ago, and the minister came himself in his own private car and took a very stiff hand in that election, with a result which was no doubt very satisfactory to himself. He went to two different points, the city of St. John and the city of Moncton, both large railway centres, where there are a large number of employees who are voters, and in both places he used to the utmost his influence to induce and force and compel the men to vote against their consciences, many of them, for the candidates which the minister favoured. That is a matter of common and notorious knowledge in the province of New Brunswick. He was successful in the constituencies in which these two cities are, and then went to a third place. In that constituency there were no railway employees under his control, and there he was not so successful. The gentleman whom he opposed there had a majority about twelve times as great as his majority in the previous election. Whether that was on account of the presence of the hon. gentleman, I know not ; but that is the fact. I merely make this statement in order that the House may not lie under the wrong impression which the hon. minister attempted to create this afternoon-an impression which could not be made in the province of New Brunswick, where the facts are so well known.

I understand the hon. gentleman to say that he knows of his own knowledge that I personally used all sorts of pressure and influence in order to coerce the men employed on the Intercolonial Railway to take part or vote in an election. Does the hon. gentleman wish me to understand that that is his statement ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is the statement 1 made, Mr. Speaker, and I reiterate the same statement now. Any person who read the speeches of the hon. gentleman in St. John and Moncton will know that my statement is exactly in accordance with the fact. The vehemence which the hon. gentleman displayed this afternoon when he was trying to urge his followers to applaud him-which as a matter of fact they seemed very loth to do-was as nothing to the vehemence he exhibited on the platform when he was attempting to coerce those employees to vote in favour of his candidates in the late provincial election.
Has the hon. gentleman any evidence or any personal knowledge of the facts other than what he says appears in reports of my speeches in the newspapers to support the statement he has made ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Those I think should be sufficient; but if they are not, I may say that the common rumour throughout the province is to that effect.
Oh, oh.
Common knowledge. Common rumour has a very great effect, you know, and is generally founded somewhat on fact, too.

With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity of saying that what the hon. gentleman has said is absolutely and entirely without the slightest foundation. I invite the hon. gentleman to take an early opportunity of reading to this House the reports of the speeches which I delivered, and I venture to say that they will not corroborate the statement he has made.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Why, Mr. Speaker, if the hon. gentleman's reputation were not so well known throughout the province of New Brunswick, the people would be shocked and surprised at the statements he made this afternoon. But knowing him so well as they do, they simply shrug their shoulders and say nothing.
If the hon. gentleman will accept my invitation, I will abide by the result.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with the greatest possible attention to every word that fell from the lips of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals when he made his explanation this afternoon. I sympathized a good deal with the hon. gentleman, because he had a very difficult task in explaining the results of his management of the Intercolonial and other government railways during the past six or seven years. He quoted a great many figures as to the increased traffic, the increased sums paid for wages, the better position of the road, and a whole lot of things which to my mind did not throw very much light on the situation. He was asked by the hon. member for South Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) during the early part of his speech to give the House some information with regard to the capital expenditure made on account of the railway, during the time he has administered the affairs of the department. I am not aware that he vouchsafed the information asked for; but there are two or three facts which stand out prominently in the administration of the hon. gentleman which cannot be too frequently impressed on the House and the country. The hon. minister made a comparison between the administration of his predecessor in the one single year, 1896, and that of himself in the year 1902. A more unfair and misleading comparison could not have been made, because, as the hon. gentleman knows, the conditions existing in Canada during the past twelve months as compared with the conditions which existed in 1896 rendered it impossible to make a fair comparison between those two years. For an hon. member to try to justify the administration of the Railway Department over which he presides, by making a comparison of the year 1896, a year of unusual depression not only in Canada but throughout the world, with a year of redundant prosperity, especially in that part of the Dominion served by the Intercolonial Railway, is certainly not what we might expect from a gentleman who has had the long parliamentary experience of my hon. friend the Minister of Railways. If he desired to be fair, he would have compared the six years during which my hon. friend from South Lanark administered the affairs of the Intercolonial Railway and the Prince Edward Island Railway, with the six years during which he has managed them. I appeal, Mr. Speaker, to the hon. gentleman himself and to every hon. gentleman who supports him, whether, if he had desired to do simple justice to the hon. member for Lanark, he would have confined his comparison to one single year ? Let me state two or three facts to the House, and I will leave the hon. gentleman to make an explanation of them. Since 1897, when the hon. gentleman assumed the management of the Intercolonial Railway, how much has he expended on capital account ? Is it not a fact that during the past six years he has expended on capital account on the two government railroads $13,890,54? ? Will the hon. gentleman deny these figures ? I obtained them from official documents, and I challenge him to say whether they are correct or not. During the previous six years, when the hon. member for South Lanark was administering those roads, how much was expended on capital account ? $2,835,691. The colossal fact stands out, and it cannot be contra-

dieted or challenged, that during the past six years the hon. Minister of Railways has expended over $11,000,000 more on capital account than his predecessor did during his six years. And what has been the result ? A colleague of the hon. Minister of Railways boasted in Toronto a few years ago that when this administration came into office they found that the western terminus of the Intercolonial Railway was in a ploughed field, and their policy was to bring the railway into the great metropolitan city of Montreal. We all hoped for good and great things from that policy ; but what has been the net result of the operation of the road since then ? During the six years in which the hon. member for South Lanark operated it, the deficits in the receipts as compared with the opera-ing expenses amounted to $949,784. If we were justified in incurring the enormous expenditures which we did in bringing the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal, and in equipping it with gilt-edged plant of all kinds, what have we reaped as the result V During the past six years in which the hon. gentleman has been administering the Railway Department, the receipts on the railway have been actually short of meeting the operating expenses by no less than $886,763. All we have gained in those six years in net results, as compared with the previous six years, has been the miserable sum of $60,000, notwithstanding the enormous expenditure on capital account.
The hon. gentleman's deficits in operating expenses during the past six years have' just been $60,000 less than the deficits in operating expenses durifig the previous six years, when the business conditions of this country were not nearly so prosperous. That is all the hon. minister can take any credit for ; and if he thinks parliament was justified in voting these enormous expenditures on capital account in order to save in six years the sum of $60,000, he may take what comfort he can from that opinion. These are facts that cannot be controverted. During the past six years he has spent $11,000,000 more on capital account than 8itl his predecessor in the previous six years, when there was not that revival of trade which has since characterized all parts of Canada ; and he has only succeeded in reducing the balance against us, as between receipts and operating expenses, during the whole of that period by $60,000. But he pleads that there are exceptional conditions in connection with the location of the Intercolonial Railway, which make it impossible to pay as well as other roads. There is the water on the one side and competing lines on the other But did not the same conditions exist before that hon. gentleman assumed the administration of the Railway Department ? Did not his predecessor have precisely a similar condition of things to contend against ? In my humble judgment, the hon. gentleman himself is between the Devil and the deep

sea in his endeavour to invent some plausible explanation, and when the people have time to read carefully his arguments, they will come to the conclusion that the administration of our railway affairs during the past six years has been extravagant, unwise and prodigal, and that they have not received the value they were entitled to from the enormous expenditure made by the hon. gentleman. Let me emphasize what has been so well said by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker). He pointed to the argument of the hon. minister that if he had charged as high rates as other roads-which rates he admitted were not unreasonable- his revenue would have been much larger. H admits, therefore, that notwithstanding the fact that this country has run into debt $16,000,000 during the past twelve years, through our capital expenditure on the Intercolonial, yet the freight rates have been lower than they might have been. In other words, that he has failed to earn money that he should have earned in reduction of this huge capital expenditure. What will the people of the other provinces think when that statement goes to them ? Should we not expect better things from this business administration than that they should have persisted in running the Intercolonial Railway at a loss ? Had we not a right to expect some better management by the hon. minister than is shown by this humiliating confession, that althougli he is running the road at a heavy loss, the rates charged on the traffic! are from 50 per cent to 100 per cent less than those charged by other lines ? That is a most astounding admission ; and I would point out to the hon. gentleman, with all possible respect, that it is his duty, under the circumstances, at the earliest possible moment, to so readjust the rates on passenger and freight traffic that at least the expenditure will not exceed the receipts. If the public debt of the country is being added to by millions every year for the purpose of operating the Intercolonial Railway, the people have a right to insist that reasonable rates should be charged ; and if the rates charged are not fair and reasonable, they should be readjusted so that the Intercolonial Railway system may cease to be a sink hole into which millions of public money are being thrown every year. I did not intend addressing the House, but I felt compelled to emphasize the fact that while, under the administration of hon. gentlemen opposite, the debt of this country for the operation of the government railways has been increased by the enormous sum of $14,777,305, we have, so far as these two reads are concerned, practically nothing to show for that expenditure.

Among the different charges. Mr. Speaker, made by the hon. member for Lannark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) and the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) against the manage-

ment of the Intercolonial Railway, there is one in particular which I think should be specially emphasized and discussed. That is the charge that the lion. Minister of Railways is deceiving the country by a false system of accounts. If that charge he true, surely there is not an hon. gentleman sitting behind the hon. Minister of Railways who would support him in this wrong-doing ? If the charge be not true, then it seems to me that my hon. friends from Lanark and Hamilton ought to withdraw it. The charge has been made by these two hon. gentlemen flatly and unequivocally that the Minister of Railways has brought down cooked accounts, and that, by a system of false bookkeeping, he has endeavoured to deceive this House and country. One can hardly iin-magine a more serious charge, and I sincerely hope that the hon. minister will either controvert it or frankly admit that he lias done wrong and promise to do better in the future. My hon. friend from Hamilton states that all railway companies properly administered charge to working expenses, the renewals of rolling stock. For instance, if a railway company, at the outset, spends a million dollars on rails, it charges that amount to capital account, but whenever a rail is worn out and has to be renewed, the cost of the renewal is charged to working expenses. The wisdom and propriety of such a course are evident even to one who is not conversant with the management of railways. But if a different system is followed on the Intercolonial Railway, if the renewals are also charged to capital account, then, in the case, for instance, of the renewal of a rail, you will have two rails charged to capital account, one of which is worn out, but both are assets. Such a system of keeping accounts is certainly not honest, and from it you can obtain an accurate idea of the value of our assets. The same contention holds with regard to the purchase of cars. If when a freight car, which was originally charged to capital account, is worn out, another is purchased to replace it, and the new car is also charged to capital account, yrou have two Items against capital account which are represented only by one asset. If you spent a million dollars on cars,, in the first instance, and then spent another million dollars to replace these, and charged each expenditure to capital account, you have/ a capital account of .$2,000,000, which is represented only by an asset, of $1,000,000. If the accounts of the Intercolonial Railway are kept in this manner, the report of the Minister of Railways, instead of being called a blue-book, should lie called a cook hook. When one thinks of this parliament, the highest court of the land, voting improperly on capital account, moneys which should be charged against working expenses, and when we find a leading official of the road declaring that he is compelled to falsify his hooks in order to make 116
them agree with the parliamentary' vote, surely parliament has no reason to be proud of what it is doing. Surely not even the most ardent supporter of the Minister of Railways will argue that it is proper for parliament to do that which, if done by a humble clerk in a financial institution, would cause him to be sent to one of our provincial penitentiaries. I am not making any charge against the hon. Minister of Railways, because I do not pretend to be conversant with the facts, lint when so serious a charge as that of cooking accounts s made against him, the hon. minister should either refute it and show that he is not keeping his books in a manner different from that followed by other railway companies, dr else bow to tbe inevitable and adopt a proper system of book-keeping.

EMMERSON (Westmoreland!. The protests that are annually offered against tbe expenditure on the Intercolonial Railway seem to me unworthy of the Canadian sentiment that ought to prevail in this parliament. I have no desire to refer to the Intercolonial Railway from a sectional standpoint, for that railway has not been, in any sense, devoted to the interests of one particular section of this Dominion. It has contributed more to the interchange of thought and the interchange of trade between the different provinces of the Dominion than any other factor we have had. In former years the people of the maritime provinces traded to the south of them across the Bay of Fundy. The building of the Intercolonial Railway contributed, to the bringing together of the people of Ontario and Quebec and the people of the maritime provinces. That seems to he forgotten; and it seems to be forgotten, as well, that the manufacturers and the merchants of Toronto and Montreal, have, by means of the Intercolonial Railway, been enabled to find a very large and profitable trade. The protests which are made against the rates that are charged on the Intercolonial Railway' are based on the idea that this is a sectional advantage. But surely the benefit of any such lessening of charges is for those living in Ontario and Quebec as yvell as for those living in the maritime provinces. We. forget, seemingly, that the Intercolonial Railway was built for a certain purpose. It was built largely as a military road, and I presume it was built where it was built because of political exigencies at the time. But it was built as part of the compact of confederation, and as a national highway, and should be treated in the same way as other highways of the country. How is it that I hear no word of protest from my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) with respect to canal charges ? Only the other day a very large and influential delegation waited upon the right hon. Premier and. in the interest of trade and commerce, in the interest of the people of this Dominion,



36S4
demanded that the tolls on these canals should be entirely removed. Is there any protest against that ? Do you hear any protest on the part of hon. members from the east with respect to the large expenditures made upon the canals and not a dollar realized to the revenues of the Dominion arising from them ? It seems to me that this is slightly unfair. It was not my intention to take part in this discussion; but when I hear hon. members refer to expenditures on the Intercolonial Railway and insist that these expenditures are largely political, I, as one having some knowledge of that field, cannot remain silent. Political influence, you say, is exercised to the detriment of the management of the Intercolonial Railway. Why, if political influence is being exercised, it is being exercised by the same men who, for eighteen or twenty years exercised that influence when their friends, hon. gentlemen opposite were in power. Fault is found with the book-keeping on the Intercolonial Railway, yet the book-keepers are the same men who were there from 1879 to 1896, and the system of book-keeping is the same as it was during that period.
A different minister.

There is the same manager, the same accountant, the same chief book-keeper-the same men from top to bottom; there has been no change. I am not reflecting upon these men at all In makiug that statement; I simply say that when you charge against this administration Or against the Minister of Railways and Canals, the exercise of political influence you are speaking of something that does not exist. I remember well when there was a change of government in 1878 and, from the head of the Intercolonial, the late C. J. Bridges, down to the very hod carrier in the railway yards at Moncton, they went out by wholesale. The general manager, also Mr. Lutt-rell, the chief superintendent, were removed and hundreds of men in the shops were thrown out of work. And why ? Because of political influence. That continued down to 1896. Any man who was suspected of having political leanings in favour of those then in opposition soon found that he had to seek some other means of livelihood, for he was not allowed to remain in the employ of the Intercolonial Railway. But, has there been a change since then ? The same men who were in the employ of the road when the change of government came in 1S96 are employed there to-day. There has been no change in the officials, no change in the workmen. I am sure that those who are conversant with the actual facts also know this-that in matters of promotion in the Intercolonial Railway it is not only men who are friends of the administration now iu power who are recognized, but all, including those who have been working tooth and nail at every election-as I know from Mr. EMMERSON.
a personal standpoint-ever since 1878, and even down to this year of grace, against the party with which I have been allied for all these years. I say that political influence, if any has been exercised, has been exercised against the present administration, and I say this as the representative of the county of Westmoreland and as knowing whereof I speak. Therefore, I protest against any idea going abroad throughout this country that the administration of the Intercolonial Railway is in any way coloured or tinged with partyism and political influence. If there is such a tinge and colour, it is not with the ' rouge,' as they say in the province of Quebec, but rather with the other colour.
Now, as to the rates on the Intercolonial Railway, they are the same as have been in force since 1878; there have been no material changes; certainly there has been no increase, and, as the hon. minister explained, the conditions are such there, by reason of water competition, that if any attempt were made to charge higher rates it would only result with loss in advancement to the road. The question of political influence is always raised against government ownership of railways. Now, there are many kinds of partisan influence, and I question whether the people of this country should denounce simply the political influence if such does exist under government ownership, as against the political influence that may be exercised in a very different way and by a very different method. I am sure the people of Canada would prefer to have the party in power exercise its political patronage- and I care not what government may be in office-rather than be throttled, by great corporations which have a peculiar method of exercising political influence, a political influence which is even recognized within the precincts of parliament. In your committee rooms when bills are under discussion, and in parliamentary debates, you recognize that political influence, and it does not arise out of, nor has it any connection with, party institutions, but it arises from the corporations of the country. There are none who know this better than hon. gentlemen opposite. It is known throughout the country, and the newspapers of the Dominion, especially the independent newspapers, teem with articles day after day pointing out these influences. I say it is far better in the interests of Canada that we should submit to any disadvantages, to any evils if there are such, arising from the government ownership of railways, than to be bound down by the pernicious influences, I would almost say the damning influences, resulting from the control of great corporations. Hon. gentlemen may wish to make a point against the administration of the Intercolonial, but they all recognize that what I am now stating is true. They all recognize that it would be far better to

submit to political influences in tbe exercise of patronage by government in the administration of a railway, than to submit to these other influences to which I have referred and which I need not elaborate.
Does the hon. gentleman make the charge that members of this House are influenced by corporations in their deliberations in this House ?
Certainly not. I am sure no hon. member would be willing to say that any such influences could be exercised.
Then what does the hon. gentleman mean ?

I mean exactly what I say. There may be an exercise of influence, of course, in a proper way, in a parliamentary way, and without any results that might be termed unpleasant ; but I am referring to the influences that are abroad in this country arising from the power possessed by great corporations. I make the point simply to show the contrast between any disadvantages there might be in connection with government ownership of railways, and the disadvantages which arise under the system which has largely prevailed in this Dominion and which prevails to a great extent in the United States. If I were to attempt to make an argument for government ownership, I might refer to a great many things which I should not mention now, but which I may have an opportunity to mention later on.
But I cannot permit this occasion to pass without entering my protest against some references which have been made against the maritime provinces. During the course of this debate there have been insinuations made that the construction of this railway and its management have been wholly in the interests of the maritime provinces and in the interests of Quebec through which the Intercolonial runs. This is my third sessio'n in this parliament, and I have listened to many discussions on the Intercolonial, but not yet have I heard my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Borden) the lender of the opposition, get up and express his views witli respect to the rates on the Intercolonial, and with respect to these denunciations which we have heard against the Intercolonial and its management as a government road. As that hon. gentleman represents the city of Halifax, it would be interesting to have an expression of his views on the points which have been raised in that direction. There are other hon. gentlemen coming from the maritime provinces whose opinions we would like to hear on these questions. They remain silent, as does the leader of the opposition, and say nothing in answer to the charges which are thus made. If the canals are established in the interest of trade and commerce, and if no tolls are charged upon these canals, why do we not hear hon. members coming from a particular section of the Do-116$
minion make that fact a subject of complaint ? I want to say that we do not hear hon. members from the extreme west indulging in any such denunciations, but they come from a confined circle, and I am thankful to say it is a confined circle. I hope that the individual members belonging to that particular circle will broaden out in their views, and look upon this matter from a national standpoint, as a railway that is serving the interests of Ontario as well as those of Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island ; I hope they will look upon it from the standpoint of a unite4 Canada. Because there may be some things in the management of the Intercolonial which may not meet the views of hon. members,, that does not justify them in attacking the Intercolonial as a sink-hole of expenditure for the whole Dominion. It is unfair to the policy which has been pursued by successive governments, it is unfair to tile founders of confederation who agreed upon that railway in the interest of the whole Dominion. They established it with the idea that it would cement together the several provinces, and it has resulted in much good in that direction.
The Intercolonial to day is, in my judgment, the best asset that the Dominion of Canada has. We have been told that the public debt has been increased to the extent of $23,000,000 by the Intercolonial. What have you to show for it ? You have your road and your rolling stock as a splendid asset. I do not pretend to be a prophet, but I believe from the bottom of my heart that within a few years it will be one of the best paying properties belonging to this Dominion. But do those hon. gentlemen who complain about the increase of the public debt on this account make any complaints against the exceedingly large outlay that was made in subsidizing the Canadian Pacific Railway ? The Intercolonial I believe represents about $60,000,000 of public money expended on its construction-and in its maintenance, if you will. But the moneys that were paid out in subsidies for the Canadian Pacific Railway exceed that sum by a very large amount? without taking into account the countless acres of land which were given in land grants to that road, lands which to-day are selling for $6 or $7 an acre and sometimes higher. We hear no complaint about that. Yet we do not own to-day a spike of that great highway, we do not own a foot of the land. The money is gone, and we are paying interest on it, and there are no complaints. I say it is manifestly unfair to the people, detrimental to the harmony that should exist between the different provinces, to make these exceptional complaints against the Intercolonial Railway.
Hon. members as a party would reflect greater credit upon themselves, and they would stand better in the country it they looked upon this subject in the way the people of the country look upon it, in the

Mr. Speaker, in connection with the working of the Intercolonial Railway, I put a question on the Order paper some little time ago which the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) asked me to replace by a motion for papers which he said would be brought down immediately it was moved. I do not think these papers have yet been submitted. May I ask the hon. minister if he has submitted the return asked for ?
Yes, I brought it down at once.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Well, it has not been reported to me. That would be of importance and I would be very glad to look at it in connection with the statement of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals in reference to the matter of rates. I am very much in sympathy with the view held by the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) and I feel that we members

from the maritime provinces cannot very well remain silent if it be broadly stated here in parliament that that part of Canada is receiving an unfair advantage in having a railway conducted at the expense of Canada generally, which is to confer some special benefit upon us. I really feel that to a very large extent in fairness to our friends from Ontario it must be borne in mind that the remarks that have been made here tonight have been elicited by the statement made by the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals himself.
How ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Because) he made the statement very broadly that the rates charged on the Intercolonial Railway were 50 per cent less than those charged by other lines in Canada.
By the two railways, the Grand Trunk Railway and Canadian Pacific Railway.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I understood the hon. gentleman to say that the rates charged in Ontario by the Grand Trunk Railway and Canadian Pacific Railway were from 100 to 150 per cent in excess of those charged on the Intercolonial Railway.
No, I said from 50 to 100 per cent.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It strikes me that an examination of the figures showing the freight rates that are charged on the Intercolonial Railway will scarcely bear out the statement made by the hon. minister. In respect to a very large part of the traffic and the revenue of the Intercolonial Railway it is quite evident that his remarks do not apply at all. That is in reference to the passenger traffic. In reference to the receipts from passenger traffic which form a large part of the revenue, I think, we in the lower provinces are paying just as much as they are in any other portion of Canada.
As to what ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The passenger traffic.
I confined my remarks distinctly to the question of freight rates. I emphasized that.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am simply calling attention-
Or rather I eliminated passenger rates from the receipts.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I think the hon. minister did that, but I wish to call the attention of the House to the fact that so far as passenger traffic is concerned, the people of

the lower provinces are not unduly favoured. They are paying rates at least as high as the rates paid in Ontario.

The hon. gentleman will at once see the force of this. Except that ail passengers from any point on the Intercolonial Railway, Moncton and east will get to Montreal for exactly the same rate, no matter how much greater the distance, as they can get to Montreal over the Canadian Pacific Railway; or from St. John over the Intercolonial Railway to Montreal, a passenger is carried on a ticket for exactly the same price as the Canadian Pacific Railway charge.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Of course the point of the hon. gentleman's observation is that the Intercolonial Railway is somewhat longer, and that the passenger is carried a greater number of miles for the same figure.
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: That is a feature which characterizes all railways in Ontario, and everywhere else throughout Canada. I think that compensation has to be made by railways that are working in .competition, one with the other. Accepting the hon. minister's explanation which is entirely in accordance with my understanding of the matter, I say that so far as passenger traffic is concerned, the lower provinces are not receiving any advantage at the expense of the rest of Canada. If the people of those provinces are unduly favoured it is in reference to freight rates, and I think in so far as local rates are concerned it will be found that they are not very much lower than they are in Ontario.
Oh, yes.
