speechtext: It has been said by the last speaker that the tariff of freight rates on the Intercolonial Railway has been the same for a number of years. I think the hon. minister will scarcely agree with that statement. He must recollect, and the country generally knows perfectly well, that when a gentleman named Mr. Harris was placed in charge of the Intercolonial Railway he raised the freight rates very considerably, so much so that the effect was a strong protest from every province where the Intercolonial Railway was doing business, and if I am not mistaken, and I am a customer of the road to a large extent, and pay freight to a large extent-
With what result ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: With the result that there was a great deal of dissatisfaction created.
With the result that the rates came down.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In some cases they did, but in other cases they remained where Mr. Harris put them.

The hon. gentleman is mistaken in stating that as a general proposition. There was a rise in rates upon certain classes of merchandise made by Mr. Harris or what was equivalent to it in the way in which the impost was made. So violent was the public clamour against that action from all parties and all sides that the tariff was reduced, put back to practically where it was before in the manner in which the carriage of the goods and the arrangement of the traffic was adjusted.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I must accept the*minister's statement because it is a matter which is entirely within his own department, but I think it is a matter of common opinion in Nova Scotia that the rates on certain classes of freight are considerably higher than they were when the minister took charge of the Intercolonial Railway. There can be no question that the freights both upon sawn lumber and logs are considerably higher now than they were before. I think it will be found that the reason why the Intercolonial Railway is making a fairly good showing to-day-and I am not at all going to abandon the argument made by my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker)-it will I think be found that the good statement made by the minister is very largely owing to the manner in which he has adjusted his revenue and his capital account. There is no answer at all to the argument made by the member for Hamilton on that point. Still, I believe that the good showing which the minister is able to make is largely because the hopes he expressed when he took over the Drummond County Railway as part of the Intercolonial Railway, have not been realized, and that he has never succeeded in developing. that large through-traffic in grain and other products which he expected. If we examine his report for the last year, it will be found that the large increases of business on the Intercolonial Railway have been made in local traffic, and that in many departments that through-traffic to which the minister looked with great confidence is diminishing. His good showing is due to the fact that he has not continued to develop the through-traffic which was being conducted at an unprofitable figure, but that he has the advantage of the enormous development in the business of Nova Scotia and Cape Breton, and in the lumber business of the lower provinces generally, which has been carried at profitable local rates. A very large proportion of the great expenditure charged to capital upon the Intercolonial Railway was made for the purpose of developing through-traffic and not for the local traffic at all. It is a reasonable criticism made upon the minister by railway men, that the

heavy engines and equipment which he introduced were not at all adapted for local traffic. The result was to place upon the road rolling stock which the road was unable to carry and which involved an enormous expenditure in the direction of improving the track, enlarging the buildings, strengthening and replacing the bridges. What is there in the circumstances of the Intercolonial Railway that would justify such criticisms as are resented by my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson)? They are unquestionably not the fact that the Intercolonial Railway was being conducted from year to year either with profit, or at a comparatively small loss to the country. During the regime of the present minister there has been a period of unexampled prosperity-as regards Nova Scotia at all events-during which for a large part of the time the Intercolonial Railway was in a state of congestion, when the sidings for hundreds of miles from the seat of activity at Sydney were filled with traffic awaiting its turn for movement, and yet in the face of all that extraordinary prosperity and that enormous inflow of business the fact remains that in the matter of deficits the present minister (Hon. Mr. Blair) shows a betterment over the history of the last six years of the Conservative regime of only some $60,000. Now, we do not like at all in the lower provinces to have any unkind criticism addressed against us or against the railway management of the Intercolonial Railway. We do not feel that it is pleasant to us to have a feeling engendered in the minds of the people of Canada generally, that the Intercolonial Railway is being conducted in such a way as to unduly favour the people of the lower provinces at the expense of their fellow citizens in the rest of Canada. Therefore it is of the highest importance to the people of the maritime provinces, that the Intercolonial Railway should be economically and efficiently managed, because the result of anything short of first-class management is to evoke this criticism. No people in Canada are so directly interested in the able economical and efficient management of the Intercolonial Railway as are the people of the lower provinces. We are deeply interested in the success of the Minister of Railways, and so far as we are concerned, we would like him to meet with the very highest possible degree of success in maintaining that road in a high state of efficiency, and presenting to this country only such favourable balances as would entirely prevent any criticism of a local character by the representatives of the people of Canada in this House. Ayhile we are ready to stand up for the Minister of Railways and to urge him to give us in the lower provinces efficient management and favourable rates, I am afraid that the protestations which the minister has made so strongly to-day in reference to the total absence of anything of a Mr. BELL.
political character from the management of that railway are not altogether borne out by the facts. I do not believe that it is possible for the Minister of Railways to make the people of the lower provinces, who are familiar with the management of that road, believe that there is an absolute freedom of anything like political pressure so far as the employees of that road are concerned. It is perfectly true, as the minister has said, that in the case of quite a large proportion of his employees they are protected against political interference by their own associations. Their orders and their brotherhoods protect them to a certain extent from the pressure which the minister may feel disposed to bring to bear upon them. I would not go so far as to say that the minister himself personally interferes, but I know that the gentlemen who represent the Liberal party in some constituencies in the lower provinces, do habitually interfere with the employees of the Intercolonial Railway, not only in Dominion elections and provincial elections, but in municipal contests, where we elect our representatives to our county councils. They do that, and they can do it successfully simply because the, people of the county in which I live and of some adjacent counties, have got the impression on their minds that when a local politician or a defeated candidate writes a letter or brings pressure to bear upon the trackman or the sectionmen or the employees of the railway generally, behind that local politician is the authority and the influence of the Minister of Railways. I would not for one moment doubt the minister ; I am perfectly willing to accept his statement, and I would like him to supplement it by making it perfectly understood throughout the lower provinces, and particularly in my own county of Pictou, that no man need be afraid of any threat addressed to him by any local politician or partisan. I trust the minister will make the people understand that behind that threat is not the authority or the power of the Minister of Railways.
I have caused that to be made known upon more than one occasion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am perfectly willing to accept everything that the minister says, but at the same time I am aware of circumstances in my own county where men have been moved about and placed at a disadvantage, when it could have only occurred because it was done in such a way that it did not reach the knowledge of the Minister of Railways, for had it been done with his knowledge he could not acquit himself of the charge of allowing political pressure to be brought to bear upon the employees of the Intercolonial Railway.

I will take this opportunity of stating the fact, that personally I gave
3C93

most explicit orders during the last Dominion election to the general manager, to notify all the officers and employees of the road that they were to be free to come and go ; that every facility was to be afforded to them irrespective of their politics to get to where they wanted to vote, and to vote according to their own wishes. The general manager had instructions to that effect from me in the most direct and positive manner during the last Dominion contest.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Would the hon. gentlemau state why Mr. Russelt left the service of the government railway ?
He wanted to go, I do not know why. I did not dismiss him.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Did he not state that political influence was used against him ?
He never stated or communicated that to me.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: He stated so publicly in the press.

I am perfectly willing to exonerate the minister, and I am familiar with the fact that he did take the course he has indicated here. Still others, using the weight of his authority, I will say entirely without his consent or desire, have brought pressure to hear to iuduce the electors not only to vote, but to do extraordinary things. I will give him an instance that occurred in the last provincial election in Pictou. The law in Nova Scotia prevents Dominion employees from voting in provincial elections. That law was adopted by the anti-confederation party in 1868, and it has been in force ever since ; and during the time the Conservative party was in power, no man who was a Dominion official or had been in receipt of emoluments from the government railway for fifteen days previous to an election ever tendered his vote. In the last election unwilling men, knowing that they were employees of the Dominion government, were forced to go to the polls and tender their votes in the face of the statute designed to prevent them from voting; and in some cases they actually took the oath which was put to them by the officials in polling places, and practically, as far as I may judge, had to commit perjury in order to do so. Does the minister suppose that these railway employees would have done that extraordinary thing unless they were doing it under the force of great compulsion ? It is not at ail likely, and I would like the hon. gentlemau to devote a little of his time, if he can do so. to an inquiry into the circumstances I am now mentioning, in order to satisfy himself whether or not the system of the Intercolonial Railway is as entirely free from political pressure or interference as he has given the House to understand that it is. I am presenting this statement without the slightest desire to give offence to the minister. I am assuming that he is absolutely truthful in what he has said : but I wish him to understand that his name and authority have been used to induce the railway employees under his control to vote ill a way in which in many eases they are most unwilling to vote. Now. I do not altogether blame the minister if he finds it impossible to be everywhere, and to know everything that is being done on the hundreds of miles of railway under his control. But if he will devote himself carefully to an inquiry into the management of some parts of the system which are not protected by the system of brotherhoods, he will find that there is absolutely no other criterion for the appointment of men on the railway than their political partisanship. I do not know one Conservative appointed on the Intercolonial since 189(1.
I am told that there have been a good many, but I am not aware of any. I do not know their politics.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am not aware of one. So far as the county of Pictou is concerned, the hon. gentleman's preserve is not invaded at all. But it is a matter of current statement that men are introduced into the service in a way that was utterly unknown in the time of his predecessors. Instead of the appo'ntments being made from headquarters, in many cases they are made by local political managers, and men are put to work on the road without receiving their appointment from headquarters. I am not making charges against the minister : I am assuming that in many cases at any rate these things are done without his knowledge. But I would like to guard him from making statements such as he has made here today, when it is a matter of common knowledge and belief in the counties through which the railways run. that there is_ no other influence exerted in appointing or maintaining in office employees of the rail-wav than political pressure. Mr. Speaker, I do not intend at this time to say anything further in criticism of the hon. minister's remarks. I shall he very glad indeed to have the return, which T understand he is to bring down, and I think it will tend to prove that any good showing made by the Intercolonial is entirely due to the fact that the business of the road has not developed in the direction that was expected by the acquisition of the Drummond Counties Railway, but that while the profitable local traffic has been developed, the unprofitable through-traffic has -not been allowed any longer to make adverse balances for the minister.

Mr. Speaker. I have listened with a good deal of interest to this debate, and if the statements which have been made are true, I think that both parties must have badly managed the Intercolonial Railway, and it is time that that railway were placed under a commission

so that we would not have this quarrelling for a whole day about its management. Now, I understood from the minister that it is not the intention to allow the government roads to be controlled by the commission which is about to be appointed. The discussion which we have had to-day has shown us plainly that the commission should have control over that railway, above all others. It seems that the book-keeping is not properly done ; but in that case one party says to the other, you are another, as the book-keeping was done in the same manner under the old regime. If that be so, it is time the book-keeping were done properly. To charge steel rails, locomotives, cars, and all that class of material which is continually wearing out, to capital account, seems to me to be a fallacy. I might ns well charge to capital account my binder that is worn out in ten years, or my plough or my harness. These things must be charged against the revenue of my farm. So all those things on the railway that become worn out. should be charged against the revenue. I know something of the history of this road. I remember over forty years ago, when the Trent affair occurred, and troops were sent over from England and landed in Halifax, this country was obliged to bring them in the dead of winter through a thousand miles of snow.
The British army was brought up from Halifax to defend our country against a threatened invasion, and the government of that day very properly considered that they should build a railway from the frontier, over which the troops might be brought at any time without interference. That was the origin, ns I understand it, of the Intercolonial Railway. I do not think it was ever pretended that that road would pay from a commercial standpoint, but I do think that the same rates per mile for hauling should be charged over it as are charged over other roads. I do not think that the Intercolonial Railway should carry merchandise cheaper than other roads carry it, but it seems to me that the only remedy for this state of affairs would be to take the road out of the hands of the government and place it under a commission. I am strongly in favour of a railway to the Pacific being built by the government. I think that it is time that this government had energy and force enough to help the people in the west out of the difficulty they are under of getting their produce to market. We know that they are severely overcharged now, but no doubt, if the Grand Trunk Pacific obtain a charter and subsidies, the men who take hold of the scheme will expect to make fortunes out of it. For my part, I do not see the need of any more Lord Mount Coxes or Lord General Booths, but we want the people to own the railway and get the benefit. With regard to the Intercolonial Railway, it seems to me that both parties have made mistakes, and it is no use in their casting slurs at each Mr. ROBINSON (West Elgin).
other. We had better right about ship aud manrfge the Intercolonial Railway better in the future, and not have it said that every man who works on it must vote Grit or be discharged. speechtext: Is it because these bridges are becoming weak through use ? He has been using them in the meantime with heavy engines, I presume. Have they ceased from use to have the strength they formerly had?
There has been no change in the system. We have pursued this system since we found it necessary to strengthen the bridges. There have been quite a number done every year.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman know of any other railway in this country that has adopted that method of strength-ing bridges ?

I have not made the inquiry, but I should be very much surprised if there were not others. The hon. gentleman may have a superior knowledge to any that our engineers possess on this question; but I cannot imagine anything that would be more defensible than doubling- up these bridges. The iron is perfectly good, the only trouble is that the bridge is not as strong as it ought to be within the limits of safety. We have been using upon the line now for two full years, and perhaps a good part of the third year, heavy locomotives, and we have in cases, over portions of the line which have these lighter bridges, been obliged to shore them up, to put bents under them and strengthen them before we could run the heavy locomotives over them. I think the general character of the alterations and of increasing the bridge structures has been of the description I have mentioned with the exception of two or three crossing large rivers such as the Miramichi and Resti-gouche. The narrower rivers and streams are crossed by these other bridges, but we have two or three large rivers such as the Miramichi and the Restigouche, or perhaps the Meta-pedia, where these spans are not used.

There must be no Presbyterians in that part of the country.
To increase accommodation at Levis, $72,000.

The same question arises there as to how far we are to go. Is this to go on year after year, or lias the hon. minister a report from the engineer showing what has been spent there and when this is going to end ? That certainly is a place where a particular work must cover the whole of the requirements. It is not a terminus. It is a station yard or something of that kind.
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I presume that work will not be done without a general report from the engineer showing what was to be done. Could the hon. minister tell us whether this will wind everything up, and if not what more we are to expect ?
The MINISTER OF RAILWAY'S anti CANALS. My impression in regard to that is that this covers the estimated cost of what is required to be done there. It is a very congested point as everybody knows who has been through Levis.
There was $75,000 spent last year.
Yes, I dare say.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Was the work done by contract ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
There was a vote of $75,000 in 1901-2, a vote of $22,000 in 1902-3, and now the hon. minister is asking for $72,000. It does not look as if he had quite known what he wanted ?
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND
CANALS. Oh, yes.
Mr. BARKER, Why do you expect- to spend $72,000 this year, when you only spent $22,000 last year ? One would have expected it to be reversed.
The work was all contemplated at the outset. The sum which I am asking it is estimated, will complete what we will have to do.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It will complete all the station works ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: What does it involve-the building of a new station ?

No, the station is already built. The situation is a very awkward one. I do not know whether all the hon. gentlemen who are within hearing are acquainted with the situation there or not. In times past, and up to the present, it has been a very dangerous situation. The station has been on the right hand side of the track, and people have been obliged to cross over these tracks to get to and from the ferry. A very great many people, particularly on the arrival and departure of trains, are going and coming across these tracks. It was found necessary that we should transfer the station to the other side. Fortunately, the present station is one that we require and may use to great advantage for freight and office purposes, so that in putting the new station on the other side, we are not by any means failing to utilize the building which has heretofore been occupied as a station. We have put the other over on the water side of the track and we have provided an overhead bridge which will enable the people to get to and from that station without crossing the tracks and without any personal risk or danger. In this item of $72,000 we estimate what the works contemplated will cost. The estimate is as follows New baggage room, $12,000 ; overhead bridge, $10,000 ; concrete platform, $14,000 ; stone curves, $1,105 ; roofs for the platforms, $30,000 ; tank, $1,850 : engineer, $3,000, making a total of $72,000, which I am advised will complete the work.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Are they let under contract after tender ?
Yes, sir.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Has the minister no architect in his own department ?
We have engineers, and as a general rule they draw the plans of all our buildings.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I see that there is $1,000 paid to an architect for drawing the plans of the Levis station.

We have no man in the department who would probably describe himself as an expert architect. It was expected that we would put up a nice presentable station at Levis, and it was thought better to secure an architect of standing and reputation to draw the plans.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There was considerable correspondence last year between the Auditor General and the minister as to the mode of auditing the accounts, which I suppose referred to the charges to capital and revenue accounts. The minister agreed to change the mode of auditing the accounts. Would he kindly say what changes have been made?

That correspondence had no reference to the question of revenue or capital account. The Auditor General seems to have been Very much impressed by the remark made by a gentleman of the opposition in the Public Accounts Committee last year, who thought it was the business of the Auditor General to audit the accounts which were paid at Moncton. The Auditor General, on looking at the statute, came to the conclusion that it was broad enough to enable him to claim the right to withhold payment of any bill until the audit had taken place by himself personally or by some officer that he might appoint. I had several conversations with the Auditor General, and I pointed out to him that this would result In a great deal of inconvenience and no public advantage, because, as the result of many years' experience at Moncton, nothing had transpired to show that the officers at Moncton had failed in the performance of their duty. I pointed out to him that we had a large auditing staff at Moncton which had been there for many years, whose sole duty it was to audit these accounts, and that if he were to audit the accounts, there was no sense at all in paying for two different audits of the same account. I submitted to the demands of the Auditor General, as we could not carry on the business of the Intercolonial Railway unless I did. He is apparently the only person in this country who is to be trusted to properly supervise expenditure and to judge as to what ought be the proper functions of government, and so I submitted with as good a grace as I possibly could. Since then there has been a great deal of inconvenience. For instance, if a sheep happens to be killed on the Intercolonial Railway and the officers inquire into it and report that the sheep ought to be paid for, it not unfrequently happens that correspondence ensues and papers are called for.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
And a doctor's certificate.
The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND
CANALS. Oh, yes ; a doctor's certificate
has to be forthcoming, and these papers oscillate between Moncton on the one hand and the Auditor General on the other ; further investigations are made, and the whole staff is set in motion in order to afford reasonable assurance to the Auditor General that this sheep is actually dead or has been seriously injured.
Or ever had an existence.
Yes. It is under those circumstances that the correspondence took place.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Is it not a fact that the Auditor General, in reply to the hon. member foivHamilton, stated that large sums of money were paid as to which he had absolutely no knowledge ? Did not the correspondence arise out of larger matters than the Minister of Railways refers to ?

I am free to admit that my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) is responsible for the present condition of things, because his remark led the Auditor General to take this view of his duties. If the Public Accounts Committee should meet again at an early date, I wish my hou. friend would withdraw the remark, so that it may be possible for the officers who are engaged in this work at Moncton to do business in a businesslike way upon the Intercolonial Railway. I confess that a great many things much larger than that have to be dealt with. I mention this to show what capacity can be found in a faithful and zealous public officer to grasp a needle as well as to strike at larger objects. One of the difficulties which we have is to get bills passed or paid at all. For a long period of years, ever since I have known anything about the Intercolonial personally, and from what I could gather from others who knew it before I came into the depai'tment, there was a recognized system of audit for printing done in connection with the Intercolonial. The Auditor General has since last session insisted that accounts for printing shall be audited and paid on the same basis on which the printing is done at the Printing Bureau. An examination of that system shows that no charge is made in connection with the investment, the cost of plant, or any of the hundred and one things that are outside of the actual labour and paper ; and there has not been for a year past a single account settled or adjusted by the Auditor.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Can this printing not be done at the bureau ?

It cannot be done at the bureau, for it is too far away, and it has never been thought reasonable that it should be done there. The claim is not that the work should be done at the bureau, but that it should only be paid for at bureau prices.

But printers cannot print at tliose prices ; they ought not to be asked to do so, and the law is not different to-day from what it has been for years. Under the law as it is now, and with the same knowledge of what it is, the Auditor has authorized the payment down to the current year of bills at the reasonable commercial price.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: After that explanation the hon. minister cannot find fault with us. He knows that the Auditor General was appointed by the Liberal government, and if he is now putting the brakes on in that way, it must be because he has not the same confidence in this government that he had in their predecessors ; and if we are suspicious in that regard, we certainly have much more reason to be so than he has. However, I would like to ask the hon. minister, whether in case of capital expenditure, for instance for rails, the old rails are disposed of and the amount for which they are sold is placed to the credit of capital account ?
Yes.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I would wish to make it remark or two on the subject of the audit. The hon. gentleman knows that the points on which the discussion occurred in the Tub-lie Accounts Committee were not at all of the nature that he has alluded to. There was no question of deciding upon a claim on a calf being killed or anything of that kind.
That is wliat it developed into.
speakername: The MINISTER OP RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I am speaking of what occurred in the committee. In one or two cases we found that after parliament bad authorized the government to spend a certain sum of money at a particular place the government spent twice that sum, without any authority whatever, and 1 asked the Auditor General how it happened that lie had passed those accounts. He said that they were all paid before he knew anything about them. Out of that arose a discussion on the question whether there was a sufficient audit. There is a departmental auditor at Moncton, but that gentleman is precisely in the position of a staff officer on a railway who can be dismissed at any time by the manager. He simply look's after the details between the departments. Such an audit is no protection to the proprietors of the railway, nor would such an audit be a protection to the people of this country. We want somebody to audit the accounts as between the public and the railway department, not a gentleman who will object to a particular item at the peril of the loss of his situation. The hon. gentleman knows that the Auditor General cannot be dismissed by the government, and for that reason matters such as I have alluded to should be audited by him. We should have the protection of such an officer's endorsement of the expenditure, not the endorsement of Hon. Mr. BLAIR.
some gentleman down at Moncton, who knows that he must do exactly as he is told, who will audit a particular account, but who will not criticise the government if it is spending two or three times what it is authorized to spend. That was what led to the discussion in the Public Accounts Committee, as the minister knows perfectly well.
Some resolutions reported.
